#2717. Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics

Sixers, Brown have a 'humbling' night in loss to Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Whatever Jaylen Brown and the Sixers dreamed up for their first matchup against the Celtics soon flew out the window on Tuesday night.

Brown was whistled for two early fouls, the Sixers fell behind and their early-season flaws were on full display in a 123-101 loss at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"We've just got to get better," Brown said. "Tonight was humbling. We got outplayed, out-executed. So we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the next one."

Over 26 minutes, Brown had 13 points on 4-for-9 shooting and five rebounds against the team that traded him away this summer.

As for the endless dissection of his relationship with former co-star Jayson Tatum, Brown didn't have much to add Tuesday. There was no public reconciliation, no obvious on-court animosity and generally nothing to satisfy fans hoping for some kind of fireworks on that front.

"I'm just focused on doing what's best for my team," Brown said. "Everything else … to be honest, I wasn't paying attention. But credit to Jayson; he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics. They executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and they were the better team tonight."

Tatum scored 21 points, two of which came on a third-quarter slam over LeBron James. Paul George continued his fantastic start as a Celtic by dropping 36 points and draining six three-pointers.

The Celtics dominated from beyond the arc, shooting 22 for 49 (44.9 percent). The Sixers went just 11 for 37 (29.7 percent) on another night of underwhelming offense. The team sits 22nd in the NBA in offensive rating, 24th in three-point makes per game and 21st in three-point percentage.

"I think that we've got some guys that are obviously shooting much lower percentages than their last season or their career average — almost a handful of guys," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "And I don't think it's because they're shooting fallaway, totally contested ones. I think they're shots we want them to take. So I think they'll continue to take 'em and I'm pretty sure those will even out into their career averages."

Joel Embiid is at 37 percent from the floor and 4 for 33 from three-point range (12.1 percent).

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center got through an injury scare when he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter and hit a three early in the third. It was his first long-range make since the Sixers' home opener back on Oct. 22.

"It's a work in progress," Embiid said. "I think the biggest thing is just not thinking. I'm probably overthinking it. The rhythm of the game is different. I'm so used to having to create for myself, so it's a little bit different.

"But I think I'm slowly getting better. You could see as soon as I made a three, the next shot in the short corner … I didn't even think about it. I just shot it and let it fly, and I made it. … I think it's just about taking what's in front of you. Make or miss, keep working on your game. It's going to get there at some point."

Even with the Sixers second in the Eastern Conference standings at 9-3, Embiid believes the team's defense has "slacked off a little bit" in recent games.

"I don't really look at the record," he said. "I just look at the process of, 'Are we getting better every day?' We can always do a better job at all phases of the game."

"They're one of the top teams in the league and they've been together for a while," Brown said. "We've got a lot to work on over here, so we've got to get to work."

The Sixers will face the Raptors on Thursday night in Philadelphia.

They'll have to wait until Jan. 21 in Boston to see the Celtics again.

"I was looking forward to this," Brown said. "I was looking forward to playing well, but s— happens. Just get ready for the next one."

#2711. Arsenal star plays for new country after 13 caps for another nation

Kepa Arrizabalaga remains the world's most expensive goalkeeper following his move to Chelsea for around €80 million, and the Spaniard now represents Arsenal. However, he has struggled to secure regular playing time at the Emirates Stadium, where he is currently the second choice.

His limited opportunities have affected his chances of representing Spain, with the goalkeeper having not featured for the national team since 2023. He made 13 appearances for the world champions, most of them in competitive matches, and at 32, his international career could be approaching its end.

Despite no longer featuring for Spain, Kepa found another opportunity to represent his homeland during the November international break. He was selected to play for the Basque Country side, giving him a chance to gain valuable minutes while his opportunities at Arsenal remain limited.

According to TalkSport, Kepa was in goal for the Basque Country during their November fixture against Venezuela in Bilbao. The match offered the Arsenal goalkeeper an opportunity to return to action and maintain his sharpness during a period when regular football has been difficult to find.

His situation at club level has become more challenging following Arsenal's elimination from the Carabao Cup. That result further reduced the opportunities available to players who are not regular starters, making the international fixture particularly useful for Kepa.

Ordinarily, a player who has represented one national team in competitive matches cannot simply switch allegiance to another country whenever an opportunity arises. Kepa's 13 appearances for Spain therefore make his involvement with another side an interesting situation.

The explanation is that Basque Country is not an officially recognised national team affiliated with FIFA or UEFA. Consequently, its fixtures are not treated as official international competitive matches under those organisations' rules.

This means Kepa was free to feature against Venezuela without affecting his international eligibility or violating the regulations governing changes of national association.

For the goalkeeper, the appearance provided a welcome opportunity to play football despite his limited involvement at Arsenal. However, he will still need to find more regular opportunities at club level if he hopes to return to the Spain squad in the future.

#2710. 6 plays that cost the Cowboys vs. 49ers

46 points. The Dallas Cowboys defense, that we know isn't very good, allowed 46 points on 9.4 yards per play. How many times can you be disappointed before you're no longer surprised? At least just once more as we saw the defense surrender multiple big plays to San Francisco.

The offense made their mistakes as well, but it's hard not to focus on giving up nearly a 50-burger at home. You can pick so many plays to choose from as to why the Cowboys lost but perhaps it's easier to choose the ones that most irritated you in watching the Cowboys lose to the San Francisco 49ers yet again. Here are the plays that should get under your skin the most and why they matter in the grander scheme.

The Cowboys looked like they had wrestled the early momentum back from San Francisco after a George Pickens score. It's not too many times the Cowboys have led by multiple scores this season and the defense has needed any possible large lead it could get.

Facing 3rd-and-8 with the 49ers on their own 26-yard line, the Dallas defense proved why. The Cowboys did a great job of putting initial pressure on Brock Purdy but he managed to scramble out of the pocket and found Christian McCaffrey as got behind the defense for a short pass from Purdy. From there he went untouched for a 74-yard score.

For a moment you felt that the Cowboys could put the pressure on the 49ers for a change but boy would that be an ominous sign of things to come.

The theme of today was one explosive play after another. If there's one thing you expect from a Kyle Shanahan offense is misdirection and out-leveraging the defense for an advantage. Deebo Samuel historically has been a thorn in the side of the Cowboys, and once again he stuck the Cowboys right where it hurts.

Samuel took a reverse pitch from Kaelon Black and raced 70 yards down the sideline for a touchdown. When you watch the replay, notice how long it takes for the defense to process what is happening. Samuel has a convoy of blockers out in front while the majority of the Cowboys defense is on the other side of the field.

What are some of the basic principles of defense at at any level let alone the NFL? Defensive pursuit and perimeter containment. That's where the Cowboys tend to struggle mightily an Samuel made them pay. One missed assignment or poor angle against a player like Samuel can turn an ordinary running play into an instant touchdown.

The Cowboys avoided letting the 49ers score points at the end of the first half before they received the second half kickoff. Down by a one point, letting the 49ers score a touchdown would be detrimental. Unfortunately, Dallas could not prevent that from happening and rookie running back Kaelon Black ran all over the defense to make a point.

The play puts another red-hot spotlight on Caleb Downs. The rookie safety was run over by Black on a touchdown that helped San Francisco seize control of the second half. Downs also had trouble finishing plays in space, including a missed opportunity to contain Purdy before the quarterback found McCaffrey for a long touchdown.

For a player with his expectations, the Cowboys need more consistency, particularly against offenses that force defenders to make decisions in space. We need to see better from Downs down the stretch.

This is where the wheels started to fall off. Sure Brandon Aubrey made two kicks beyond 50 yards. However, Aubrey hasn't been as automatic anymore and now you sometimes have to hold you breath if he can make the routine kicks.

With Cowboys looking to take seven-point lead, Aubrey missed the extra point. This left the Cowboys chasing points for the remainder of the game. With the game going the way that it did, any points at all were needed. Dallas had an unsuccessful two-point try in an effort to make up the difference after Aubrey's miss.

Aubrey has also had kickoff penalties this year and onside kick attempt at the end of the game wasn't nearly good enough. There's something off with Aubrey, and whatever it is, it is hurting the Cowboys.

For all intents and purposes, this was the last straw. The Cowboys fought tirelessly to get back in the game but fell short on defense. After Prescott connected with Ryan Flournoy for an 11-yard touchdown on fourth down, Dallas had reduced San Francisco's lead to 38-32 with 3:42 remaining. The Cowboys needed one defensive stop to give Prescott a chance to win.

Instead, just 10 seconds of game clock later, Purdy found McCaffrey for a 66-yard touchdown on second-and-10. San Francisco added a two-point conversion, extending its lead to 46-32. This was arguably the most decisive moment of the game. Dallas had finally pulled within one possession, only for the defense to surrender another enormous touchdown immediately.

After the Cowboys drew the score to 40-46, it was longshot that the Cowboys could get the ball back with enough time to take the late lead. Quinnen Williams who has been one of the few bright spots for the Cowboys defense almost came up huge.

Looking to drain the remaining time off the clock, the 49ers handed the ball of to Kaelon Black. Williams darted through the 49ers offensive line to meet Black in the hole. Williams was able to dislodge the ball from Black's arms. The Cowboys had a chance to recover the ball before Black quickly regained possession for the 49ers.

If the defense can't be average, the least it can be is opportunistic and Williams almost gave that much when the team needed it badly. The Cowboys scored 40 points and still found a way to lose. That's the frustrating reality of this team. Dak Prescott threw five touchdowns, George Pickens delivered three scores, and Quinnen Williams nearly gave Dallas one final opportunity to steal a victory.

Yet none of it mattered because the defense couldn't stop San Francisco from producing one explosive play after another. At some point, these breakdowns stop being isolated mistakes and become the identity of your football team. For Dallas, that point may have already arrived.

Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson led a game-winning drive in the fourth quarter on Sunday, which isn’t surprising given the way the 2026 season has unfolded in Cleveland.

#2708. Aaron Glenn could become sixth coach to start 0-9 in division

Jets coach Aaron Glenn has a 5-21 record during his one-and-a-half-year tenure with the team. That’s bad.

Here’s something worse: Glenn is 0-8 in AFC East games.

That’s the longest active losing streak in the division by any team. And it’s one game short of putting Glenn in a small club that no one wants to belong to.

A loss on Sunday to the Bills would make Glenn the sixth head coach since the 1970 merger to start his career 0-9 in division games. The others were Jim Schwartz (0-10), Matt Eberflus (0-9), Pat Shurmur (0-9), John McKay (0-9), and Jim Ringo (0-9).

With each additional loss, the question becomes whether it will be Glenn’s final loss. The clock seems to be ticking toward an in-season termination. Or, if owner Woody Johnson doesn’t decide to make a move before Week 18, an abrupt parting of ways after the season ends.

#2707. Manchester City & Me: Joe Corrigan Q&A

Manchester City will be celebrating former players club, Once a Blue, at our matchday against Fulham this weekend.

This Saturday, we'll be shining a light on the work they do as well as welcoming our stars of yesteryear to the Etihad for the Cottagers clash.

We'll be publishing a host of content in the build-up to the game, starting today with a insightful Q&A with City legend, Joe Corrigan.

I played football when I attended St Joseph's Primary School, but when I passed my 11-plus exam it meant going to Sale Grammar - and that was a rugby school. The only time we were allowed to kick a ball was at break times and lunch-time.

I played as a second-row forward for the school team and won county honours for Cheshire and looking back, playing a sport where the emphasis was on using my hands gave me a good grounding to become a goalkeeper, especially when I was involved in line-outs and you had to try to take the ball at its highest point.

But football was always my first love. My Uncle Tommy took me to Sale Amateurs and I was playing against grown men at the age of 14 in the Altrincham and District League, but in a strange twist of fate it was only when I left school and took an apprenticeship with the engineering firm AEI in Trafford Park that my life suddenly turned towards professional football.

A fella came up to me after I'd played in an inter-departmental game and asked I'd be interested in going for a trial at one of Manchester's big clubs. I thought he was on a wind-up. I'm sorry to say that I don't even remember the chap's name because I thought he'd been put up to it as a joke. Then I got a letter off (City chief scout) Harry Godwin inviting me to a trial game!

It meant getting a bus into Manchester, another one to Maine Road, and a third out to Cheadle Town's ground, but I'd have walked there if they'd told me to. I was signed initially as an amateur in 1966, but when it became clear that night-time training sessions clashed with my studies at evening school, my dad told me I had a decision to make. I chose football but because I was three months too old to be signed as an apprentice, I was given a pro contract. That was in January 1967 and the following October I made my senior debut against Blackpool in the League Cup. I had to get the bus to that game as well! There were plenty of ups and downs.

It was a steep learning curve. Everybody knows about Colin Bell, Francis Lee and Mike Summerbee - and rightly so because they were world-class players. But City had a team packed with talent and later that season they were crowned league champions. Tony Book, Mike Doyle, George Heslop, Alan Oakes, Glyn Pardoe, Tony Coleman and Neil Young were all at the top of their game - and don't forget that we had a magnificent manager in the boss (Joe Mercer) and a coaching genius in Malcolm Allison.

I played behind Tommy Booth during my trial game and we ended up becoming team-mates for the next 14 years. Later, players like Tony Towers, Ian Bowyer, Derek Jeffries and David Connor came through the youth team. We also had three very good goalkeepers ahead of me in Harry Dowd, Ken Mulhearn and Alan Ogley and I learned so much from them. Because I didn't have a traditional football apprenticeship, I had to learn on the job, and they were brilliant with me.

I made my league debut against Ipswich in March 1969 and a few months later, I was Harry Dowd's understudy for the FA Cup Final. Unfortunately, those were the days when teams could only name one substitute, so I went to Wembley only to watch us win another trophy. But the following season was a real breakthrough year for me.

It was the kind of thing I didn't even dare to dream about. Having said that, before I'd even signed for City, I remember being on the bus near my home in Sale Moor when I spotted two United players, Tony Dunne and Pat Dunne sat a few seats away. Can you imagine two first-team players for Manchester United on the top deck of the 111 these days? Pat was an Irish international goalkeeper, and for a reason I still can't explain, I said to him 'I'm going to be a top keeper myself.' Lord knows what he thought, but he smiled politely and I went on my way. A few years later, I was in the City team that beat United 4-0 at Maine Road in my first derby!

We also beat United in the League Cup semi-finals over two legs and when we came from behind to win against West Brom in the final at Wembley, I had my first winner's medal. I was really nervous before the game and I think Malcolm (Allison) spotted it because when we arrived at the stadium, he told me to go straight down the tunnel on my own to have a look around. It was an amazing sight, even though the pitch was a muddy mess because the Horse of the Year show had been held there a few weeks earlier.

Malcolm was right. Having a walk around on my own, even though Wembley was virtually empty, really settled me down. That was Mal's secret, for me, he really understood players. He once told the press that I was good enough to become the next Frank Swift! I didn't believe that for a minute, but when someone like Malcolm Allison says that about you, it doesn't half make you feel good.

Winning the European Cup Winners Cup in Vienna a couple of months later was the icing on the cake. Looking back, winning all three domestic trophies and a European competition in the space of three seasons makes that City team one of the very best there's ever been. I'm not sure Joe Mercer and Malcolm Allison get enough credit outside Manchester for what they achieved.

That's the life of any footballer, but especially when you're a goalkeeper. And when you're a young goalkeeper, mistakes are an occupational hazard. It's all about how you deal with those setbacks. You have to be aware that there's always a bump in the road waiting to knock you off track.

The 1969/70 season is the perfect example of that. I was capped by England at Under-23 level as well that year, but I also made a massive mistake for City that still gets replayed on TV more than 50 years later. I might have got away with a few critical headlines in the next day's newspapers in normal circumstances, but when we played West Ham at Maine Road in March 1970, the Match of the Day cameras were there because Jimmy Greaves was making his debut for them.

I kicked a clearance downfield after Tommy Booth had thrown it back to me and then made the cardinal sin of turning my back on the ball. I didn't see Ronnie Boyce volley it straight back as I made my way back to the goal at the old Scoreboard End of the ground - but I did get a glimpse of the ball as it sailed into my net. We lost the game 5-1 and I've never been allowed to forget it. For a few years it seemed to be part of the 'What Happened Next?' round on 'A Question of Sport' every other week!

But after the game came a moment that has also stayed with me ever since. I was getting a rollocking in the dressing room when I was asked to go up to the boardroom. Players weren't usually allowed in there, but Bert Trautmann had watched the game as a guest of the Club and he wanted to give me a piece of advice that I came to fall back on during all the tough periods of my career. Bert told me that every goalkeeper made mistakes but it was how they reacted to them that made the difference. He explained some of the low points he'd faced and said that putting mistakes behind you immediately made it easier to deal with the next one.

Bert was one of my boyhood heroes, along with United keeper Harry Gregg. He kept in touch with me constantly from that day and I owe him a debt of gratitude I can never repay. But what I did do, when I later became a goalkeeping coach myself, was pass the knowledge I picked up from people like Bert.

I had a wonderful career at City, but there were some difficult times and I like to think the fans appreciated the fact that I never threw the towel in. There was a time, after the Club had just paid £100,000 to sign Keith Macrae in 1973, that I thought my future might lie elsewhere because that was a record fee for a keeper. But I stuck at it and came through the other side."

It's absolutely true - although I wouldn't recommend it! I broke my jaw in a training game during the 1973-74 season and I had to have my jaw wired for about three weeks. The upside - if there was one - was that I could only eat fluids and I ended up losing almost two stones in weight. I felt leaner than I had been for years and I then worked like crazy on my fitness. I made sure that if I got another chance, I would grab it with both hands - pun intended!

Tony Book being appointed manager was another turning point. After I'd won my place back in the team, I only missed one league game in five seasons, playing in another successful City side. Twelve months after thinking I was on my way out of the Club, I was in the team that beat Newcastle to win the 1976 League Cup. Talk about a change in fortune.

'Skip' built a formidable team. Me, Mike Doyle and Tommy Booth were still there, and so was Willie Donachie. Dennis Tueart, Dave Watson, Asa Hartford and Joe Royle had been signed two or three years earlier, and then Brian Kidd came in. With youngsters like Peter Barnes, Gary Owen, Paul Power, Kenny Clements and Ged Keegan coming through we had a side to be reckoned with.

If Colin Bell hadn't suffered a terrible knee injury I truly believe we would have won the title in 1977. Liverpool pipped us by a point, but you can't tell me that having a fully fit Belly wouldn't have got us over the line.

I suppose I have to - even though the game still rankles with me. I was voted man-of-the-match by a newspaper in the first game and then won the BBC award in the replay.

We were the better team on the Saturday. I wouldn't say I felt unbeatable that day, but I did think it would take a fantastic strike or a fluke to get past me. In the end it was a fluke, when Glenn Hoddle's free-kick took a deflection off Tommy Hutchinson and sent me the wrong way. I think I would have saved it quite easily if Tommy had stayed where he was in the wall.

John Bond (City's manager) had wanted to station a man on the post because Hoddle was so accurate from set-pieces, but I told him having someone there would cause more harm than good. When Tommy heard Glenn tell a team-mate which way he was going with the free-kick, he moved around the back of the wall to block the shot. I had no chance with the deflection.

Tommy was distraught. I had to pick him up off the turf and pat him on the back. What else could I have done? We were disappointed with the 1-1 draw and the replay was a game too far for us. Gerry Gow, who had Hoddle, (Osvaldo) Ardiles and (Ricky) Villa under control in the first match, had injury problems and just couldn't raise himself physically for the replay.

My annoyance isn't about Hoddle's goal or Spurs winning the replay. But I think the game should have been decided on the Saturday one way or the other. It should have gone to penalties. I was hardly an expert at saving them, but given the form I was in that day, I would have backed us to win a shoot-out. It still hurts that one.

No. It's a question I've been asked a few times down the years and I always say the same thing. I'm a proud Englishman and I cherish every one of the nine caps I won for my country. It's the pinnacle of any footballer's career.

But I played in the era of Peter Shilton and Ray Clemence. When I first started out, Gordon Banks was England's No 1. They aren't just three of England's greatest-ever goalkeepers, they are three of the best goalkeepers to ever play the game.

So I've always been philosophical about my international career. Jimmy Rimmer and Phil Parkes were two more contemporaries who might argue they were around at the wrong time because they only won one England cap each.

When an envelope dropped through our post box with the Royal Coat of Arms embossed on the front, my first thought was that I'd been landed with a tax bill! When I read the letter inside I just burst into tears. I couldn't believe it, a lad from a council estate in Sale awarded an MBE. Even now, I can get choked up thinking about it.

I was honoured for my charity work rather than my football career, but for me the two always went hand-in-hand. When I was a kid, I had osteomyelitis in one of my knees and there was a danger that I might lose my leg, so I have always felt a debt of gratitude to doctors, nurses and anyone who dedicates themselves to looking after other people.

As a player, we were always encouraged by the club to go on hospital visits or help with charity events, but for me it was never a chore. I do those things because I want to do them.

The day of my investiture at Windsor Castle was perfect. I was more nervous than I'd ever been when I was called forward to meet Prince William, but as soon as he said he'd been told I was once a very good goalkeeper for Manchester City, that put me totally at ease. He's a football man himself, of course.

As a Club, Manchester City have been transformed beyond all recognition since 2008, but the one thing that's always been a constant since I first walked through the door at Maine Road 60 years ago is the unbreakable bond that anyone who has pulled on our famous shirt will always share.

Being a professional footballer is the best job in the world, but just because someone has been able to live that dream it doesn't automatically mean they are going to be financially secure for life, live in a luxury home or drive a big car.

Everyone has a different story. They might have financial problems because of injury or bad advice, issues with their health or mental illness. What everyone who has played for Manchester City needs to know is that they have old friends at the Club who are there to help them and their families. That's at the heart of what we do, but it's a social thing as well, knowing that you've got friends you can meet up with.

Those of us who are still around are grateful to players from the past like Steve Fleet, Roy Clarke, Alan Ogley and Fred Ayre. I succeeded Francis Lee as chairman and in 2024, the association was rebranded 'Once A Blue.' Since then the likes of Paul Lake, Ian Brightwell, Peter Barnes, David White, Richard Edghill and others have carried the baton. The support on offer to former players and the charity work that's been undertaken has got better and better.

I've been succeeded as chairman of 'Once A Blue' by Ian Brightwell and I'm now a Life Vice-president. Look, I won't be around forever - none of us will - but I do know the future is in very good hands. The support and assistance we get off the Club is exceptional and our ambition is to give the best support for any former player who needs it.

#2706. NFC West Recap: 49ers hang 46 on Dallas; Rams rout Cardinals, Seahawks win

The San Francisco 49ers put up the most points and yards in franchise history for a road game, which is also the most yards the Dallas Cowboys have given up at home.

I'm just getting started on stats. We'll begin with the 49ers averaging 9.4 yards per play. That do anything for you? How about Brock Purdy going 22-of-28 for 389 yards passing and three touchdowns, finishing with a passer rating of 154.5. Then there's running back Christian McCaffrey, who had 223 yards from scrimmage and three scores.

And yet, they still, STILL had to recover an onside kick to win the game.

Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott threw five touchdown passes, while cornerback Deommodore Lenoir spent most of the afternoon chasing Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens. Renardo Green left with the same back injury he dealt with all week. There hasn't been much about Green's status for next week as of this writing, but Kyle Shanahan said he was already playing hurt.

It was 38-32 in the fourth quarter. All points were by the offense. No sacks (well, there was one, but I wouldn't call it "legitimate" outside of the stat sheet), and the Cowboys were coming back. Then this happened:

And even then, this thing wasn't over until the most entertaining fumbleroosky play in recent memory as the clock ticked to zero:

Regardless of whether we want to be optimistic or skeptical, the 49ers stay the NFC's No. 1 seed, a game ahead of the 7-2 pack of the Detroit Lions, Minnesota Vikings and Chicago Bears. The Seahawks and Rams both won, so the division lead stays at 2.5 games. The 49ers face a tough gauntlet, starting with the Vikings. Any questions you have about this team are about to be answered over the next four games.

After trading quarterback Kirk Cousins to the Vikings on Tuesday, the Las Vegas Raiders gave Fernando Mendoza his first NFL start. At first it looked like an upset, but then the Seahawks had to spoil the party.

There were moments, however. On Seahawks quarterback Drew Lock's first dropback, he tried to shovel the ball away to avoid a sack and fumbled. Mendoza scored on a quarterback draw a few plays later, and the Raiders led 10-7 at halftime. The second half belonged to the Seahawks, with highlights like rookie running back Jadarian Price scoring his first career touchdown to take the lead, and a 71-yard Jaxon Smith-Njigba score.

Final: 21-13. Smith-Njigba had 144 of his 171 yards receiving in the third quarter alone. Just like against the 49ers last week, the Raiders had a terrible second half with negative yards until their final possession. Mendoza took six sacks as well. The score could have been worse. Lock lost a second fumble when Zach Charbonnet ran into him on a play-action fake, and Jason Myers missed a 44-yarder. Right tackle Abe Lucas left with an ankle injury, which is worth watching before Seattle comes to Levi's Stadium in Week 12.

It was a lot of Seattle things, and then a lot of Raider-ing. Unfortunately, Seattle things usually don't end in losses the way Raider-ing does.

Minshew Magic is gone to IR. That led us to Carson Beck starting for Arizona. A rookie, Carson Beck.

So what happens? The Cardinals tried doing what worked last time they played the Rams: field-goal-ing them to death. This time, it wasn't as successful, as they managed only six points throughout the game. Besides Matthew Stafford's early-game interception to linebacker Cody Simon, it was all Los Angeles. Beck threw an interception just before halftime, and the Rams turned it into a 17-6 lead at the break.

Final: 34-6 in Glendale, the Rams' fourth straight win. Arizona finished with 123 yards of total offense: 89 net passing and 34 rushing. Beck was sacked five times, 1.5 of them by Aaron Donald. Stafford threw three touchdown passes. The Cardinals need to get through 2026 and make a football team next year.

Credit where it's due: the Rams look like a team again. They're 1-2 in the division, and their bye week comes before a Thanksgiving Eve game against the Packers. No credit is given to them for getting a team like the Cardinals, a team that beat them solely on field goals a few weeks back. Luckily, the Rams also have a tough stretch coming up: the Green Bay Packers and the Kansas City Chiefs.

The 49ers "host" the Minnesota Vikings (7-2) at Estadio Banorte in Mexico City on Sunday Night Football. The Vikings traded a 2027 third-round pick for Cousins, and he went 21-of-31 for 207 yards passing and two touchdowns in a 30-10 win at Lambeau. So they got the offense figured out; what about the defense? Well, they sacked Jordan Love eight times.

Just a reminder, that's not the Cowboys defense: Dallas sacked Purdy five times, and the 49ers still scored 46. This time the 49ers' defense has to carry its share. The No. 1 seed is on the line, and Minnesota won the last two meetings. Cousins also became the first quarterback since at least 1950 to start for two different teams in consecutive weeks, and last week's start was against the 49ers, when Jaden Dugger returned his pass for a touchdown. At least the game isn't in Minnesota.

The Rams and Seahawks are on bye. So, bye.

The Cardinals visit the Kansas City Chiefs, who beat Atlanta 35-13 behind five Patrick Mahomes touchdown passes. Gotta love it when the 49ers get Atlanta's best, but then they go back to doing Falcons things.

#2705. Panthers pull out 20-17 win in New Orleans, take lead in NFC South

NFC South football has earned a negative reputation over the last few years and Sunday’s game between the Panthers and Saints didn’t do much to change that, but it did push one of the teams into first place in the race to represent the division in the playoffs.

After the Saints rallied to tie the game on a Charlie Smyth field goal with 41 seconds left to play, the Panthers took over on their own 34-yard-line. Bryce Young threw an incompletion and then uncorked a deep shot to wide receiver Jalen Coker. Saints corner Kool-Aid McKinstry was flagged for pass interference and that set up a 54-yard field goal as time expired.

Ryan Fitzgerald had missed from 48 yards in the first half, but he nailed this kick and the Panthers are in first place after a 20-17 win.

There’s some irony in the fact that a penalty helped put the Panthers in position to win the game. Carolina committed 17 penalties during the contest, including a facemask call on linebacker Tyrel Dodson that helped set up Smyth’s game-tying kick.

The Saints did their best to match that sloppiness with a pair of turnovers in the first half and they focused on the running game well beyond the point when it became clear that they weren’t going to generate the kind of production needed on that front. Travis Etienne, Audric Estime, and Alvin Kamara combined to pick up 24 yards on 17 carries on Sunday.

Their offense picked up a bit once they leaned on throwing the ball and rookie wideout Jordyn Tyson wound up with 11 catches in his second game of the year, but the overall approach was still lacking against a Panthers team that has not been very stout defensively this season.

New Orleans will be in Chicago next Sunday and they’ll need a win there to try to keep themselves in stalking distance of the Panthers heading into the stretch run.

Carolina improved to 4-5 with the win and they will host the Ravens in Week 11. They’d be wise to continue leaning on Chuba Hubbard in that contest. Hubbard had 27 carries for 92 yards and two touchdowns along with five catches for 80 yards. That accounted for 172 of the Panthers’ 283 total yards, so Carolina’s best chance of winning games appears to be relying on their workhorse running back.

#2704. Celtics’ historic start against Mavericks proved plenty: ‘We got a really, really good team’

BOSTON — The Dallas Mavericks stood no chance coming into TD Garden on Sunday night. It only took the Boston Celtics 12 minutes to make that abundantly clear.

The Celtics outscored the Mavericks 42-9 in the first quarter. No, that's not a typo. It was the largest first-quarter point differential in franchise history and the biggest margin in a single quarter since the Los Angeles Lakers outscored the Sacramento Kings 40-4 in 1987.

"We got a really, really good team," Jayson Tatum said after Boston's 131-94 win. "And I think it really just starts with our depth. Especially in that fourth, fifth spot of whoever we want to come in and start. Whether it's Hugo [González]. Whether it's Baylor [Scheierman]. Whether it's J-Walsh. Ron [Harper Jr.], all those guys are interchangeable, more than capable."

Dallas entered on the second night of back-to-back, without Kyrie Irving, and coming off brutal consecutive road losses to the Minnesota Timberwolves and Cleveland Cavaliers — in which they allowed an average of 130 points, the most they've allowed back-to-back this season.

Boston entered riding a five-game winning streak with the best record in the Eastern Conference, fresh off three days' rest and with a squeaky-clean injury report.

From the jump, the difference between the two teams that crossed paths in the NBA Finals just two years ago became glaringly apparent.

The Celtics made 16 of their first 27 shots, including seven of their first 13 threes. The Mavericks, ice-cold as soon as they came out of the players' tunnel, opened the game 2-for-18, missing all eight of their 3-point attempts. From there, nothing changed.

At least nothing significant enough to turn the tide.

Dallas found somewhat of a rhythm from long range, knocking down five 3-pointers in the second quarter, then again in the third to cut Boston's lead down to 25 points, but that was as close as the Mavericks ever got to sniffing a competitive ballgame.

Nov 15, 2026; Boston, Massachusetts, USA; Waiting for play to start up during the second half against the Dallas Mavericks are (left to right) Boston Celtics guard Ron Harper Jr. (8), guard Hugo Gonzalez (28), guard Devin Carter (99), center Luka Garza (52) and guard Baylor Scheierman (55) at TD Garden. Mandatory Credit: Winslow Townson-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

For Boston, concerns about maintaining double-digit leads were a non-factor. Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla believes focusing on protecting a lead misses the bigger picture of what his team is truly honing in on.

"It's not about hanging onto leads," Mazzulla said. "That's a passive mindset. It's not about building on them. It's understanding the ebbs and flows of the game and constantly answering the questions: Are we playing well? Having a good process? Or are we not playing well? And that's something you learn over the course of the season."

Tatum was the only Celtic to play over 25 minutes, logging 30:08, giving Mazzulla plenty of leeway to unleash Boston's depth. González, Scheierman, Harper, Luka Garza and Devin Carter each played at least 12 minutes, combining to score 35 points off the bench.

Their ability to easily insert themselves into action remains a part of the team Mazzulla will never look past.

"They don't care about who starts, who finishes, 10 minutes, 24 minutes," Mazzulla said. "They just impact winning. They're not distracted by any nonsense, and they understand that any night they can do something different that gives us a chance to win — whether it's guarding the other team's best player, whether it's rebounding, whether it's crashing on the offensive glass. Those guys take pride in having a role on our team that's necessary to get to where we wanna get to."

In the closing seconds of the fourth quarter, with Boston's lead hovering around 40 points, Scheierman dove headfirst toward a loose ball that eventually went out of bounds. Mazzulla and the rest of the Celtics' bench immediately rushed over to help him up.

That best reflected the standard Mazzulla and his coaching staff expect from this group, playing until the final buzzer regardless of the score rather than easing up when the outcome appears decided.

Even Maine native Cooper Flagg was impressed.

"Just the level that they were competing at," Flagg said. "You know, something that we need to look at and look in the mirror and decide if we're competing at that same level. And if we want it as bad as they did, and I don't think we did."

Flagg continued his praise of Boston: "I feel like we weren't competing at a high enough level, and that's kind of been — over the last three games on this road trip — what it's been. So taking that from them. Just we gotta compete at a high enough level."

The Celtics checked just about every box on Sunday night:

Shoot 41.8 percent from 3-point range on 55 attempts: Check.

Build a double-digit lead and never relinquish it: Check.

Hold Flagg to 17 points on 33.3 percent shooting and a minus-30: Check.

Run Dallas into the ground and give the end of the bench some extended minutes: Check.

Limit every starter (besides Tatum) to fewer than 25 minutes: Check.

It was the most dominant version of this Celtics team we've seen all season.

Tatum's smiles in the locker room suggested he and his teammates know it: They've got something special brewing in Boston. That doesn't mean they'll score 130 points, hold an opponent to nine in a quarter and run teams into the ground every night.

#2703. Joe Burrow becomes the MVP favorite

Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow is having a potentially historic season. And, to no surprise, his performance has vaulted him past Bills quarterback Josh Allen as the favorite for the NFL MVP award.

After registering a fifth straight game with four or more total touchdowns — matching Peyton Manning (2004) as the only two players to ever do that — Burrow has surged to a +105 favorite to win the MVP trophy.

Along the way, the Bengals blasted the Steelers, 38-18. Burrow completed 35 of 44 passes for 409 yards and four touchdowns, as Cincinnati outgained Pittsburgh, 484 to 222.

Allen is second in the current odds, at +310. 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy lurks at +400, with Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence at +500.

There’s a gap after those four, with Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes at 16-1. (Seahawks receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who arguably best fits the official Associated Press definition of the term, remains an 80-1 long shot.)

The voting, which happens in the days after Week 18, will undoubtedly be influenced by the final configuration of the AFC and NFC playoff trees. Getting the top seed will give the quarterbacks of those teams a boost.

In the AFC, rhat could be the Bengals. Or the Bills. Or the Jaguars. Or the Chiefs. In the NFC, it could be the 49ers.

For now, Burrow has laid the foundation for a stretch run that earns his first career MVP award.

#2701. 5 Bears Takes: Grading The First Half and Dissecting The NFC North

Following a fast and furious nine games, the Chicago Bears enjoyed their bye over the weekend. In the process, they watched two divisional foes beat each other up and got a live look at their Week 11 opponent as the Panthers beat them at home. The playoff picture continues to take shape, and the Bears will start practice early next week as they gear up for a second-half run. We'll cover all of that, and more in a special installment of 5 Bears Takes.

1. Grading out the offense over the first nine games of the season.

Before the season, head coach Ben Johnson spoke about wanting to set the NFL's scoring record. While some took those words and ran with them, the Bears were well on pace after a Week 1 that produced 59 points on the road. Since that point, the offense has yet to break the 40-point mark again, but they've eclipsed the 30-point mark four separate times. All of which were with starting quarterback Caleb Williams under center.

Through nine games, the offense ranks within the Top 5 in yards per game (383), Top 10 in points per game (26.8), 11th in EPA/play, and 10th in success rate. In total, their numbers are right around where they sat for the majority of last season, with one major caveat: They missed their starting quarterback for a third of the season (so far). They've also faced four of the Top 10 defenses in the league through that stretch.

Overall, there's still plenty of meat left on the bone when looking at this unit's production and what it could (or should) be. With better health at the quarterback position and no clunkers in the second half of the season, the Bears have a real opportunity to finish as a Top 5 offense. Part of that will depend on health at key positions like running back and receiver, but the offensive line will play a key part, too. We've seen multiple flashes of dominance, but there's still plenty to clean up, especially when it comes to penalties and self-inflicted mistakes. With a better-than-expected defense, they've been able to control most games, but for them to take the next step and be scarier down the stretch, the offense must be more consistent.

2. Grading out the defense over the first nine games of the season.

Coming into the season, the defense felt like the Achilles' heel of what could be a Super Bowl contender. During the offseason, the front office did very little to improve the defensive line, and through the first month and a half of the season, it seemed clear the interior defensive line wouldn't be good enough. Despite what their depth chart has looked like on paper, they've performed better than expected, even before the acquisition of defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons.

Through nine games, the defense ranks 1st in third-down percentage (22.8%), Top 5 in fourth-down percentage (30.8%), Top 10 in EPA/play, yards per game, and sacks, and gives up just 20.4 points per game. It's also worth mentioning that they were 9th in pressure percentage coming into Week 10. With Simmons in the mix on the interior, the biggest hole this group has is at cornerback. The hope is that with a healthy Malik Muhammad, either Jaylon Johnson or Tyrique Stevenson can step into the spot opposite the rookie and provide consistency and stability. With any luck, they'll get Coby Bryant back at some point in December. It's worth pointing out how well Cam Lewis has played since taking over the starting spot opposite first-round rookie Dillon Thieneman.

With the divisional defenses starting to shake out, this group must continue its upward trajectory. Getting back Dayo Odeyingbo should help the defensive line, but Austin Booker, Montez Sweat, and even Grady Jarrett have been noticeably better since the arrival of Simmons. Many expected the Bears to make another move or two before the deadline, but with nothing materializing, they're stuck with what they have. Similar to the offense, health will be key down the stretch, but overall, the team should feel pretty good about where they stand. The only real concern heading into the second half is how well their cornerbacks can perform against top offenses.

3. Dissecting the NFC North after another hectic week that saw the Bears drop from first to third place.

With the Bears' bye week, they were the only team in the division that was not in play on Sunday. The Detroit Lions took their crack at the piñata that has become the New England Patriots in the early-morning slot, and outside of the opening drive, it wasn't much of a game. The Patriots lost quarterback Drake Maye early, and, to put it nicely, backup quarterback Tommy DeVito was ineffective. For as impressive as the Lions were, they lost another star defender when Aidan Hutchinson went down with what appeared to be a serious knee injury following a sack of Maye on the first drive. The play (and subsequent celebration) took two of the most impactful players out of the game before it could really even get going. Although the Lions have been playing much better defense as of late, losing their top two leaders, Jack Campbell and Hutchinson, will wear on them as the season goes on.

During the next time slot, the Packers hosted the Kirk Cousins-led Vikings. What looked like a good matchup on paper turned into a season sweep for Minnesota, following a 30-10 drubbing. The Vikings' defense continues to be one of the best overall units in the league, and with Cousins under center, the offense looked more cohesive, even if it wasn't a perfectly played game. Cousins has plenty of familiarity with the offense, so it's fair to assume that he'll continue to hit the ground running. For the Packers, it's hard to know whether Sunday's 20-point loss was simply a bad day at the office, or a sign of things to come. Green Bay has shown clear holes all season, and although they've looked considerably better over the last month, there are still ways to attack them.

All in all, the division once again had another winning week. With the Lions and Vikings both winning, there's a three-way tie at the top with all three teams sitting at 7-2. The Packers will go on an abbreviated bye week before going to Los Angeles to face a red-hot Rams team on Thanksgiving Eve. Ultimately, their bye week will amount to the same number of days off as it would if they played on Thursday night and then played a Monday night game the following week.

It's clear that all four teams are playoff-caliber, but it remains to be seen if all four can make the playoffs come January. With Sunday's results, the Packers have now fallen a game and a half behind everyone else, while sporting a 1-3 record within the division. Even more troubling is that their 4-4 conference record won't help them much in tie-breakers once more games are played. Heading into Week 11, all four teams fill out the seven teams that would comprise the NFC playoff picture, but with plenty of head-to-heads remaining (both in the division and the conference), this is still a long way from a resolution.

Heading into Week 11, here's how the divisional standings look:

Lions win the head-to-head tie-breaker against the Vikings and have a better divisional record than the Bears.

Vikings win the head-to-head tie-breaker against the Bears.

After Week 11, each team will have seven games remaining. Both the Bears and Lions have favorable matchups, while the Vikings will play the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday Night Football. Barring a surprise, the Packers will find themselves a full two games back of first place. It's just a matter of how many teams will be sitting at 8-2 by the conclusion of next Sunday. It's also worth noting that Green Bay and Minnesota have just two divisional games remaining, while Detroit has three, and Chicago still has four.

Taking it a step further, here's how the remaining strength of schedule plays out for all four teams in the division:

For a division with four of the Top 7 teams in the NFC, each team's remaining strength of schedule all rank within the Top 10. In other words, buckle up, because this race is far from done.

4. Taking a deeper dive into the NFL playoff picture: The AFC is taking shape, while the NFC is still a nine-team race.

As we turn the page on Week 10, the playoff picture is truly taking shape in both conferences. The elite teams seem clear, as do the handful of teams that are all but out of the playoff picture. There aren't many middling teams in either conference, but there are more in the AFC than the NFC through 10 weeks. Taking a deeper dive into each conference, each race is becoming clear.

On the outside looking in: New England Patriots (5-5), Baltimore Ravens (4-5), Las Vegas Raiders (4-6)

The top of the AFC is loaded with top-tier teams. The Bills are tied with the 49ers for the best record in the league at (8-1) and have a favorable schedule down the stretch. In the AFC West, the Chiefs hold the tie-breaker over the Broncos, but with both games already in the books, it'll come down to whoever has the best divisional record. The loser of the West should take the fifth seed. The Jaguars and Bengals are both also sitting at 7-2, and an argument could be made for either team being right up there with the Bills. Barring a surprise with Jacoby Brissett under center, the AFC North looks like a two-team race, with the loser grabbing the sixth seed. The seventh seed will likely come down to the Browns and Patriots, but the Ravens have an outside shot if they can field a better offense. A few weeks ago, I would have taken the Patriots to earn that final Wild Card spot, but with their injuries and how bad they have played over their last two games, it feels like a true toss-up between the two. The Browns are a younger team and maybe aren't as talented as the Patriots, but sometimes the season's context matters. Houston's loss on Sunday against the Browns all but shut down their slim playoff hopes.

Flipping over to the NFC, it's a similar story, with a handful of clear "top teams." Yet, unlike the AFC, there's going to be a division winner (or two) who will finish with a worse record than most (if not all of) the Wild Card teams. While the 49ers currently hold the No. 1 seed, they'll see a handful of playoff-caliber teams over their final eight games. Here's a look at the current NFC playoff picture:

On the outside looking in: Seattle Seahawks (6-4), Los Angeles Rams (6-4), Dallas Cowboys (4-6)

While many had the 49ers as a potential playoff team, it's hard to imagine that anyone had them with a commanding two-game lead in a division with the defending Super Bowl Champions and this year's overwhelming Super Bowl favorites. Yet, here we are. Not only are the 49ers 8-1, but they are 3-0 within the division. Ultimately, they are likely to win most tie-breaking scenarios within the division, but they still have games against Minnesota, Kansas City, Seattle, and Los Angeles. The NFC North is a gauntlet, and that doesn't appear to change any time soon. There are still plenty of head-to-head matchups that will help shape the final standings, but for now the Lions hold the tie-breaker over both Minnesota and Chicago due to their divisional record (and head-to-head). I'm still not convinced all four will make the playoffs, but right now it seems like a good bet they'll send at least three. The Packers vs. Rams on Thanksgiving Eve will be big for tie-breaking purposes, as both teams come off bye weeks. The NFC East and NFC South are both disasters. We'll see if the Giants can maintain a record above .500, but the winner of the South seems less likely to hold that honor. Ultimately, the last three playoff spots will come from the North and West. The Cowboys have an outside chance, but at this point, that's likely more a divisional conversation than anything to do with the Wild Card.

Barring some great surprises, it could be argued that at least 10 of the 14 playoff teams are already "set". We'll see how the back end of each Wild Card race settles, but outside of that, the NFC South is the only division that is really up for grabs and could add or subtract someone from the overall playoff picture.

5. A second-half look ahead: With eight games remaining, what's the magic number to not only make the playoffs but secure a second consecutive NFC North title?

As highlighted above, the Bears head into their final eight games of the season with the hardest remaining schedule in the league based on current records. For reference, the .630 winning percentage is almost .200 points higher than the winning percentage they have faced in their current schedule. It's also worth mentioning that this includes a three-win Saints team on Sunday and a one-win Dolphins team in Week 14.

At 7-2, Chicago's current playoff probability sits in the high 80s, according to The Athletic and ESPN. They hold a game and a half lead on the trio of the Packers, Rams, and Seahawks, while already holding the head-to-head tiebreaker over Seattle.

Ultimately, 11 wins should get the Bears into the playoffs, but it's highly unlikely they'll outright win the division like they did last year. While they sit at 5-2 in the conference right now, their only two losses have come within the division. To make matters worse, they are the only team in the NFC North without a divisional win, after losses to the Vikings in Week 1 and the Packers in Week 5. The good news is that they still have four divisional games remaining. The bad news is that three of the four matchups will come over the final three games of the season.

Assuming they take care of business and beat the only two teams currently under .500 that they'll play, that would leave them at nine wins. Add in two divisional wins, and that leaves them at 2-4 within the division. Thus, the chances of 11 wins being enough to earn another NFC North title seem highly unlikely.

Finishing at 11-6 would mean a 4-4 finish, which in the grand scheme of things wouldn't be a terrible finish considering their strength of schedule. Matching their win total from a season ago with a harder schedule could be seen as a win, but it would also likely lock them into a Wild Card spot. While some look at potential matchups as the fifth or sixth seed and see the winners of the NFC East and NFC South, that's just one round of the playoffs. Having to win three games on the road to get to the Super Bowl is not impossible, but it's highly unlikely.

It's clear that the Bears are one of the better teams in football, but their remaining schedule will make it hard to finish with the type of record that will ultimately reflect how good they are as a team. With that being said, a 3-1 finish in the division, coupled with winning against the Saints and Dolphins, might be good enough to get the job done.

Here's how the schedule looks over the final eight games of the season starting Sunday:

While 4-4 would be "acceptable," the baseline over their final eight games should be a 5-3 record. Sure, it won't be easy, but 2-0 against below .500 teams and 3-1 in the division would get it done. If they go 2-2 within the division, a split between AFC juggernauts could also make sense. The Bears likely won't be favored in all of their games, but that doesn't mean they won't have more than a fighting chance in each one. Some matchups are more favorable than others, but as we've learned with this team so far in 2026, they can beat anyone. 12-5 might be enough to win the division, but a 13-4 record might be good enough to not only lock down the North but also push them into the No. 1 seed, depending on how San Francisco looks down the stretch.

Overall, it's safe to say that six out of the final eight games will have a playoff-like atmosphere, and although they'll only have three standalone games in this stretch, I would not be surprised to see the Jaguars or Lions game flexed before Week 18. No matter how it shakes out, this team is in great shape not only for the division, but also to be primed for a Super Bowl run. They'll have plenty of stiff competition in front of them, which will help once January rolls around. Embrace the difficulty, and just know that most of these games will feel like standalone playoff games over the next eight weeks.

#2700. Inter Chronicle - Diary of the season | October - November 2026

Night has already fallen, and has been with us for at least an hour. Autumn is beginning to take hold, and you can feel it in the air, not just by looking at the calendar. You can sense it in the electric atmosphere at San Siro, which had been waiting quietly for almost a month to turn Nerazzurro once again. The long international break had only made us long for Inter even more, as we looked forward to the first month packed with fixtures, battles and football. Looking at the calendar, we knew this game against Parma would be the first of nine matches crammed into 30 days, the opening fixture in a run of games that would put our ambitions to the test and show us what shape our dreams could take. We get through it with ease, in just over half an hour. The team takes to the pitch full of fire, adrenaline and relentless energy. Just 13 minutes are enough to bring the first roar from the stands, as Petar Sucic wins the ball and fires home. It happens so suddenly that even the cameras miss it: some fans only realize we've scored when they hear the stadium erupt. Two minutes later, we're back in the opposition box, with Esposito on the ground clutching his heel. A VAR check is needed before Calhanoglu is sent to the spot, where Hakan displays his trademark composure. Then, in the 31st minute, Mkhitaryan and Thuram combine to make it three. The goalscorers from the Scudetto-clinching game on May 3rd are celebrating against the Gialloblù once again, giving us a wonderful flashback. A through ball from Mkhi, a right-footed finish across goal from Tikus, into the same goal and the same corner. 3-0. The second half is all about control and attacking intent, entertainment and game management. Spence makes his debut, earning his first applause with a few bursts of pace down the right to get the engines going. Night has already fallen, but we're back, ready for a month in which we'll meet every three days for our next appointment with Inter.

A strange, topsy-turvy, rollercoaster of an evening. Our first European night at San Siro, the emotional spark as the anthem rang out, and the roar of the Meazza as the final words echoed around the stadium: "The Champions!" Club Brugge came to Milano ready to take us on, playing with courage and organisation. Both teams went toe-to-toe, and the intensity was off the charts. It was the visitors who struck first: Forbs broke forward at pace and was brought down in the box by Calha. Tresoldi made no mistake from the penalty spot. We responded with a wonderful move, finished off by Lautaro. At half-time, it was 1-1, with the game still wide open. After the break, the match turned into an almost relentless game of ping-pong, with the action swinging from one end to the other. Amid all those exchanges, two pivotal moments ultimately shaped the game. Lautaro found himself one-on-one with Sommer, feinted to shoot and sent the goalkeeper to the ground, but when he finally got his shot away, the ball was slightly trapped under his feet and he couldn't quite place it where he wanted. The Swiss goalkeeper reacted brilliantly to save with his foot. At the other end, a defensive mix-up gave Tresoldi a clear path to restore Club Brugge's lead. It was a heavy blow that left us reeling, and another soon followed: the Belgian side kept pushing forward and creating chances, before Tresoldi found himself with another ball to tap home and complete his hat-trick. But Inter are the comeback kings. El Toro was still there, ready to lead the charge and keep believing. In the 81st minute, he scored again to bring us back into the game. San Siro erupted for the final 10 minutes, but in the 87th, Vermant was sent through on goal and slotted home the visitors' fourth. Was that the knockout blow? No. We still had something left. Bonny's late strike in stoppage time gave us hope, and we threw everything forward in a desperate attempt to find another goal. But when the final whistle blew, the score stood at 3-4.

"My dear friend, I'm writing to you to take my mind off things for a while." Lucio Dalla's L'anno che verrà rings out beneath the tower of the Dall'Ara at the final whistle of Bologna vs. Inter, a scene that has brought us mixed emotions in recent years. Not this time, though. Our players embrace and celebrate in front of the Nerazzurri section. It is a powerful display of strength and character, bouncing straight back after that turbulent Champions League night. It takes us a little while to get going, however. Pobega puts the hosts ahead after 10 minutes, and their intensity causes us a few problems. We even come close to conceding a second. But these are precisely the moments when character comes to the fore: the ability to stay in the game, the determination to fight and overcome adversity. Marcus Thuram sweeps those problems aside with a thunderous header of breathtaking beauty. It comes in the 44th minute, just moments before half-time. Meeting Barella's driven cross, Tikus rises to extraordinary heights and powers his header into the far corner. He doesn't celebrate. Instead, he calls us to order and urges us on. It isn't the first time, and it won't be the last. Going into the dressing room at 1-1 is a breath of fresh air. We regain our confidence, and our quality begins to shine through. We spoke about sliding doors against Club Brugge. This time, those turning points open the way to all three points. In the 69th minute, Chivu brings on Diouf and Carlos Augusto, who combine to produce the comeback goal just 49 seconds later. A move full of quality, heads up and movement perfectly timed: Andy picks out Zielinski with a clever through ball, having already spotted Carlos's run towards the far post. A low cross, and all that is left is to tap the ball home. Perfectly executed. We don't want to take any risks now; we want to finish the job. Calhanoglu, Mkhitaryan and Bonny also come on, bringing fresh legs, intelligence and even more quality. They are the architects of the third goal, with Carlos providing the assist and Ange-Yoan applying the finish. Another comeback, another victory: heads held high, courage restored and three more points to banish the fear.

There is a moment when everything seems bleak. Fatigue begins to take its toll, spaces are hard to find, and doubts start to creep in. Will we finally get our Champions League campaign up and running? Tempers begin to flare, with a few heated exchanges on the pitch. San Siro rises to the occasion, embraces the challenge and turns up the volume. Every tackle is met with a roar; the crowd erupts at every ball won and every throw-in earned. The atmosphere reaches fever pitch when the referee shows Bastoni two yellow cards in the space of just a few minutes. In the 68th minute, we are down to ten men. San Siro becomes a cauldron, and now we need every ounce of courage we have. Once again, the team comes together when the going gets toughest. Shakhtar move the ball around with their trademark Brazilian flair, but it is the Brazilian in Nerazzurri colors who decides the game: the all-action, all-purpose Carlos Augusto. He wins the ball on the edge of our own box, launches the counterattack and surges forward as if there is nothing left to defend. A blistering, unexpected, lightning-fast run that catches the opposition defence off guard. The ball moves from Zielinski to Mkhitaryan as Carlos continues his sprint through the middle. The Armenian picks him out with a wonderfully weighted through ball, a delicate left-footed pass that floats over the last defender and drops perfectly into Carlos's path. Brazilian technique, as we said: a chest control, followed by a left-footed finish into the corner to put Inter ahead, and a slide in front of the Curva to cap a sprint worthy of a 100-meter champion. His teammates rush over to join him, and the stands go wild. The closing stages are all about resilience and togetherness, before a roar of unrestrained joy erupts when the referee blows the final whistle. Our first Champions League win: a night that began in darkness has turned wonderfully Nerazzurro.

"Homo faber fortunae suae," wrote the Roman author Appius Claudius Caecus in his Sententiae. Man is the architect of his own destiny. There are times when this saying rings truer than others. Take this late-October Sunday lunchtime, for example, which is proving decidedly hard to stomach. In the 90th minute, Fiorentina are leading 1-0 at San Siro. This time, it really seems too late to turn things around, and bad luck has certainly played its part. We've been denied by the crossbar and by De Gea, an insurmountable last line of defence for the Viola. They took the lead through a stunning Jimenez strike into the top corner. So, how do we get out of this? We are the architects of our own destiny, after all. Marcus Thuram takes those words literally. He's tried everything throughout the game, but as stoppage time begins, he still has more to give. He bursts into space, drives towards the edge of the box, combines with Diouf and unleashes a left-footed shot with the precision of a billiards player sinking a perfect shot. 1-1, in the 91st minute. We're back to life, the pulse is racing, and there's still the rest of stoppage time to come. Could it happen again? Fiorentina retreat into their own penalty area as we throw everything forward. Chivu has also brought on young Lavelli to add more firepower up front. In the final minute, a cross is sent towards Lavelli. He can't quite reach it, but Thuram is waiting behind him. Tikus gets ahead of Valdepenas, who has no choice but to bring him down. The reaction when the referee points to the spot is indescribable. Marcus is pure adrenaline: he jumps to his feet, fired up, and celebrates wildly in front of the Curva. His face transformed, his energy absolutely ferocious. Zielinski steps up to take the penalty. We hold our breath as he begins his run-up. A powerful right-footed strike, straight under the crossbar. What a roar from San Siro, and what incredible emotions our Inter gives us. We've done it again. We are the architects of our own destiny.

We arrived at the Penzo still riding the adrenaline from Sunday. The boost from our win over Fiorentina could provide a huge lift as we faced our first midweek fixture of the season. We had taken control of our own destiny against the Viola by believing until the very last chance. But here in the lagoon, we found ourselves bogged down. The adrenaline gave way to the cold air blowing in from the sea. Venezia were compact, solid and intense, combining defensive organization with quick and dangerous counterattacks. They made life difficult for us, had a first-half goal ruled out by the narrowest of margins, and then saw Provedel produce a miraculous save. Our energy seemed to be fading. We tried to move the ball around, but the spaces simply weren't there. We needed to find a way to win this game, but the minutes were ticking away relentlessly. We needed a moment, an opportunity to seize. Just one would have been enough. Instead, we got two. Scrappy, perhaps, but both came from our determination to claim all three points, to keep running and never stop, even when our legs were giving out. In the 80th minute, Thuram bursts down the left and drives into the box. His low cross takes a deflection off Moreno and rolls into the net. We're ahead, but it's not enough. Two minutes later, we win a corner, again from the left. Calhanoglu delivers, Carlos Augusto gets a touch at the near post, and Halal turns the ball into his own net. Venezia's resistance is finally broken, and we're 2-0 up. We see out the closing stages and can finally breathe a sigh of relief. It had seemed impossible to pick the lock, but we never gave up. Even on a day when our energy appeared to be running low, even when our usual sharpness deserted us, we head back to Milano with another three points.

Unfortunately, it wasn't to be. We can only shake our heads and reflect on what might have been. The final whistle in the derby confirmed our first league defeat of the season, following a difficult game in which we were caught cold. Milan were clinical, making a fast start and going 2-0 up inside the opening ten minutes: two chances, two goals. But, as always, we responded. We began to play our game, pressing higher and attacking down the flanks. We won a series of corners and set pieces, and it was from one of those corners, in the 22nd minute, that we got ourselves back into the match. Akanji flicked the ball on at the near post, freeing Bastoni inside the six-yard box. Alessandro met it with a close-range header to make it 2-1. We were back in it, with plenty of time still to play. Inter began to turn the screw as Milan retreated deeper, and an equalizer seemed only a matter of time. In the 33rd minute, Carlos Augusto sent a low, driven cross in from the left. De Winter failed to make contact, and the ball fell to Spence, who struck it first time with his left foot, driving it into the ground. Maignan looked to have been caught off balance, but somehow managed to get a hand to the ball and turn it just wide. It was a turning point, and this time it went our opponents' way. Because, despite continuing to press and dominate possession, we were caught again in the 44th minute. Moreira scored directly from a free kick to make it 3-1 just before half-time. This time, the comeback never came. The second half ticked away, and our hopes gradually faded. We had lost a Serie A match for the first time since March. But defeats are always an opportunity to pick ourselves up and go again.

So we pick ourselves up. And we do it straight away. De Kuip is a fierce atmosphere, and Feyenoord are a young, talented side, but we need to get back on track. The right mindset, concentration and character: it doesn't take long to realize that our night in Rotterdam will mark a turning point after a difficult spell. We're determined, we hit the ground running, and it takes a moment of brilliance to break the deadlock. Bisseck curls a left-footed effort from the right-hand edge of the Dutch side's penalty area, sending the ball on a beautiful arc into the far corner. What a strike, Yann! This is the Inter we know: pressing and aggression, quality in possession and attacking transitions. Zielinski dictates the tempo, Thuram is always one step ahead of his opponents, and Spence is a constant threat down the right. It is his assist that sets up the opening goal, and he also plays a key role in the second. He bursts forward, throws in a couple of feints and sends in a low cross that takes a deflection and loops into the air. The ball drops at the far post, where Pio Esposito is waiting. A header, off the crossbar and in. A roar of relief and joy, his first goal in our colors in more than a month. Finally, Pio! A goal to get him going again, to celebrate, and to swing the game firmly in our favor. The third goal is another gem, further proof that, for Zielinski, it makes little difference whether he shoots with his right or left foot. A thunderous left-footed strike finds the corner after clipping the inside of the post, extinguishing Feyenoord's hopes just after the restart. From then on, we manage the game with maturity: fresh legs, rotation, control and recovery. A wonderful and hugely important night, a valuable victory in our European campaign, which is back on track after a difficult start.

The perfect way to bring this run of games to a close, to say goodbye to San Siro before the international break, and to send a message to ourselves and our opponents. The weather is turning colder now, and night falls earlier. During Inter-Parma, darkness had arrived around half-time; for Inter-Como, it was already dark when the match kicked off. The atmosphere, however, is electric. The Meazza is packed and roaring, and the team is shining from the opening exchanges. We push high, pressing, winning the ball back and denying Como's midfielders time and space to play. We want to attack, we want to score. Dimarco wins possession on the left in our own half, setting in motion the moves that lead to the opening goal. The ball is quickly switched to the right, Thuram drives forward and takes on his man before finding Spence on the overlap. A low cross, and Pio is there to turn it home with the instinct of a true goalscorer. Arms aloft, biceps on show, and a Nerazzurri roar. We're ahead in the 12th minute, and double our lead in the 19th. This time, the cross comes from the left, delivered by Zielinski. It's a fierce, dangerous ball that Valle misjudges and fails to clear. His attempted clearance falls straight to Thuram's right foot, and from close range, he makes no mistake. In a split second, as the ball reaches him, he unleashes a devastating finish into the net. Then Tikus takes a seat on the advertising hoardings, unveiling another iconic goal celebration. Twenty minutes of dominance, quality football and a superb Inter performance. Just as against Feyenoord, the team then seems to go on autopilot: continuing to press when the opportunity arises, staying compact when required and giving the opposition no openings. Total concentration, not a single detail left to chance. The game ticks by, the Meazza applauds, and we can finally catch our breath. A long, demanding month is coming to an end, with nine matches played in 29 days. The record stands at seven wins and two defeats, but beyond the numbers, we've experienced a month of incredible emotions: fear, joy and every aspect of what it means to be Inter. After the international break, another packed schedule awaits: nine more matches in 31 days, from November 22nd to December 22nd, as we look to bring this Nerazzurri year of 2026 to the best possible conclusion.

#2697. Cubs free agent target: Ryan Jeffers

Carson Kelly, who's been very good behind the plate for the Cubs the last two years, is a free agent.

So the Cubs need another catcher to pair with Miguel Amaya.

Personally, I'd just take Kelly back for another year, maybe sign him to a deal with an option for 2028/buyout clause.

If Kelly won't go for that, I think the Cubs need to examine the FA market, because the team's top catching prospect, Owen Ayers, has played only 33 games at catcher above Double-A and likely needs some more Triple-A experience before joining the Cubs full-time.

So let's look at Ryan Jeffers, another free-agent catcher. Jeffers was the Twins' second-round pick in 2018 out of UNC-Wilmington and has spent his entire seven-year MLB career with Minnesota. In 2026, he put up pretty good offensive numbers, batting .256/.353/.461 with 14 home runs in 92 games. The missed games were due to a hamate bone fracture in his left hand. Those injuries can occasionally sap a player's hitting ability, and Jeffers' numbers did go down from .295/.408/.541 in 37 games pre-injury to .231/.317/.410 in 55 games after his return. The pre-injury numbers were a bit of an outlier compared to previous years so I'd say Jeffers' overall slash line of .242/.327/.426 is probably more representative of what he'll hit going forward.

Jeffers is about league average in throwing out runners, and won 62 percent of ABS challenges — but didn't make many, just 13, winning eight of them. He turns 30 in June, so he's about three years younger than Kelly.

MLB Trade Rumors projects Jeffers at four years, $75 million and The Athletic has him at three years, $45 million. I think the latter is more realistic for a catcher of Jeffers' age and abilities. Personally, though, I'd rather have Carson Kelly back. This article in The Athletic says the Twins have "genuine interest" in a reunion with Jeffers.
