#2675. What The New Jersey Devils Should Focus On During A Rare Quiet Week

Times are good for the New Jersey Devils and their fans. After weathering a category five hurricane of backlash from 200 hockey men over the Connor Hellebuyck saga this past week, the Devils brushed off the loss in Winnipeg to win both ends of a crucial home-and-home against the Washington Capitals. While not on the same level as the Carolina Hurricanes, the Caps have given New Jersey some trouble since the pandemic-shortened 2021 season. So to win both games in regulation was massive, not only for the sake of the standings, but for the mental aspect of slaying a dragon of sorts. The Devils saved Hellebuyck for these two contests, and he rewarded his new team by making sure the eight-point swing went entirely in the favor of the Devils.

And now, after seven games in 11 days, after enduring the mental burden of navigating the Winnipeg situation, after yet another wave of illness has depleted the roster, the Devils have finally hit a bit of a lull in the schedule. They only have two games this week: Wednesday at home against the Montreal Canadiens, and Saturday on the road against the St. Louis Blues. The break is needed for a number of reasons. First and foremost, as Sheldon Keefe alluded to in his postgame speech on Thursday, his team is, in his words, "running on fumes". It's not great to hear that after only 25% of the season is done, but this relatively light week should help the team recharge the batteries, especially considering the team got two days off after the game in Washington on Saturday.

Second, despite the results, there are definite areas of concern that demand addressing. It's something that Keefe himself has acknowledged over the last week, even as his team continues to rack up points. I assume that after the two days off, Keefe will hold a rare practice for his squad on Tuesday. And with two days between the Montreal game and St. Louis game, I imagine there will be a practice mixed in there as well. And even if there isn't as much on-ice practice time as I might think, I have to imagine that there will be plenty of deep dives into the tape, the statistics, and the scouting reports to help clean up whatever needs to be cleaned up.

So with that being the case, let's explore some areas that New Jersey can focus on during this uncommonly mellow week.

We have to start, of course, with the biggest area of concern with the team at the moment: the penalty kill. Jared did a deep dive on this last week if you want some in-depth analysis of this problem. But in a nutshell, the PK has not just been bad, it has been near-bottom-of-the-league bad. Entering today, New Jersey's penalty kill is ranked 30th in the league at 66.0%. That figure is ahead of only the Seattle Kraken and Vancouver Canucks, meaning the Devils have the worst PK in the entire Eastern Conference.

I wonder if Anton Silaev can provide a jolt here. Jonas Siegenthaler (1:43), Brett Pesce (1:36), Dougie Hamilton (1:35), and Brenden Dillon (1:25) are the top four defensemen in shorthanded time on ice per game. Of those players, Siegenthaler has by far the best Expected Goals Against per 60 at 4.81. Pesce (8.19), Hamilton (6.63), and Dillon (10.32!), are just not cutting it. Silaev has the potential to be a defensive god in any situation. I might not be a hockey expert per se, but I do know that a 6'7" defenseman with a wingspan the size of Hobby's Deli that has remarkable four-way mobility can be a huge (pun intended) asset on the PK. Keefe did give him 40 seconds of shorthanded ice time in his NHL debut on Saturday, and I wonder if giving him regular penalty killing duties can help pull the Devils out of their shorthanded malaise.

This one is simple. After conceding the first goal in their first five games of the season, the Devils have been doing a much better job of flipping the script. The "1-0, Them" scars were finally starting to heal after that ugly stretch to begin 2026-27, but lately the issue is starting to creep back into their game. It hasn't been egregiously bad, but the Devils have allowed the first goal in four of their last seven matches.

The good news is that the Devils have won three of those four games. But that's not exactly a sustainable way to live. Over the long haul, the Devils need to get back to hopping out to strong starts. How exactly does one practice that? Well, I acknowledge that it's not exactly a straightforward thing to work on. Some of it does come down to luck as well. But I also feel as though a lot of it is a mindset thing. If I were Keefe, I would reiterate to his team that they need to get locked in from puck drop. Not two or five or 10 minutes after puck drop, as soon as the puck hits the ice. A lot of games could be at stake over it.

From the start of games to the ends of them, the Devils are starting to develop a third period problem. Here are the 5-on-5 Natural Stat Trick numbers over their last seven third periods:

Aside from the Oilers and Islanders games, the Devils have had a lot of trouble in the final frame lately. And even in the matchup with Edmonton, they got outscored in the third period anyway. The good news here is that, despite all the bad numbers in the above table, New Jersey is still outscoring their opponents 10-7 in the third period over that stretch. But that won't last much longer if the Devils continue to get buried in the run of play.

I'm not sure if the fix here is tactical, or if the team just needs to regain their energy after an arduous stretch of games. Either way, they need to relearn how to finish strong in a hurry, or we could see a prolonged losing streak in the near future.

Lost in all the Hellebuyck drama in Winnipeg and the subsequent Hellebuyck vindication over the two games against Washington, Jake Allen just hasn't been himself lately. On the season, he has an .881 save percentage in 10 games played. According to Natural Stat Trick, Allen is in the red when it comes to Goals Saved Above Expected, sitting at -2.90. That figure is 51st out of 76 goalies league-wide. Moneypuck's metrics are even more unkind, dinging Allen for a -5.70 GSAA, which is 68th in the league.

Whether you're going by the advanced numbers, the traditional numbers, or the eye test, Allen has not been his usual reliable self this season. I still have faith in him to be a quality backup to Hellebuyck. 10 substandard games does not shake that belief in him. But whatever he needs to work on to get his game back, he needs to work on it a lot this week.

I doubt he will play on Wednesday, but considering the Devils follow up their Saturday game in St. Louis with a Monday game against the Columbus Blue Jackets, I can see Allen getting the nod against the Blues to give Hellebuyck plenty of rest in preparation for a division game. But whenever we see him next, Allen will be well-rested with plenty of time to have ironed out the kinks in his game. This week will be key to those efforts.

We will end where we began: special teams. Unlike the penalty kill, the power play has actually improved lately. Thanks to a pair of PPG's in Washington on Saturday, New Jersey has climbed to a 20.6% conversion rate on their power play, good for 19th in the NHL. That's still not great obviously, but it is a significant improvement from ranking in the mid-20's with a success rate in the mid-teens.

But there's still work to be done. I would like to see Dougie Hamilton get some run with PP1. I also wouldn't mind seeing either Arseni Gritsyuk or Timo Meier get a shot on the top unit either, most likely replacing Jesper Bratt. Meier in particular showed his power-play worth in the last two games. On Saturday, he parked himself at the net-front and muscled home a Gritsyuk feed for a big power-play marker. Just the sort of greasy goal a power forward like Meier specializes in. And on Thursday, he showed he isn't just a one-dimensional scoring threat either, threading an outstanding cross-slot saucer pass to Evan Rodrigues for a PPG.

Aside from personnel shakeups, I would also love to see PP1 work on being more decisive with the puck. There has been too much perimeter work on the mad advantage, with the Hughes brothers and Bratt playing catch on the outside, trying to open lanes that just won't open. Crisper, faster, and less predictable puck movement would do wonders for the unit's success rate.

Again, it's been better lately so it's hard to complain too much about this. But despite the recent improvements, there is still plenty of work to be done to get the power play right.

Just looking at the recent results, I wouldn't blame anyone for thinking this is all a little too harsh. After all, New Jersey has won seven of their last eight, 11 of their last 13, and 13 of their last 16. Those are remarkable results, and most of that has been earned with stellar all-around play. But that doesn't mean that the Devils should be complacent, and listening to Sheldon Keefe after the Saturday game, it doesn't sound like they are, which is great news. This is still a high quality team that has absolutely crushed their first quarter of the season. But if New Jersey wants to make sure their second quarter is just as good as their first, they'll need to do some fine tuning. There are other areas of improvement aside from the ones we've discussed today that warrant attention, but these ones are the most important concerns in my opinion. Get these right and make sure there are no other areas of decline elsewhere, and the Devils will be just fine.

What do you think of the first quarter of the season? What is your opinion on the areas of concern we've indentified today? What other improvements would you like to see the team make? What do you expect in the second quarter of the season? As always, thanks for reading!

#2673. Bucks vs. Hawks Player Grades: Jakucionis notches career high, Trent proves he’s worth every penny

Despite leading by as much as 22 in the second quarter, the Milwaukee Bucks just couldn't go the distance with the Atlanta Hawks, losing 113-106. As I get into later, the "up by 22 points" thing was mostly the result of unsustainable shooting, so I didn't see this game as some choke, but it's fair to wonder how that big a lead could have dissipated so quickly. On balance, if you remove their horrid second quarter—which they lost 37-16—this was probably one of Milwaukee's best games of the year. They showed real resolve, made multiple comebacks, and gave themselves multiple chances to tie the game at the end. Unfortunately, the Bucks simply could not make the crucial play. Read our full summary of the game here and catch a six-minute audio recap on the Bucks+ podcast, Bucks In Six Minutes, below.

26 minutes, 25 points, 5 rebounds, 5 assists, 3 steals, 2 turnovers, 9/16 FG, 4/10 3P, +7

The Hawks ran a switch-everything defence, and the Bucks had basically no answer for it until Jakucionis came in. His speed and burst were the perfect antidote to that defence, unlike other players—coughTyler Herrocough—who operate with more finesse. I loved basically everything about Jakucionis' game, who dropped a career-high 25 points. He was decisive with the ball, knowing when to pass, dribble, or shoot. He also made a major impact on defence, picking up full court and making his man work; he even had that possession in the fourth where he forced a turnover in the backcourt. Also, a hat tip to KJ for the passion he played with; this Bucks team can sometimes be a bit lifeless, and it felt like he came in with an agenda to bring energy no matter what.

20 minutes, 8 points, 5 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 steal, 5 turnovers, 2/13 FG, 0/5 3P, 1/1 FT, -12

Herro was awful. As I just alluded to, he does not have a lot of burst in his game, which is fine when he can pick on one weak defender, whether that be a guard or a big, but the Hawks just had nobody to attack. Herro had nothing, so he resorted to BS foul-drawing and hoping for calls. Had some bad off-ball defensive possessions too. Easily his worst game of the year.

30 minutes, 6 points, 5 rebounds, 4 assists, 2 steals, 5 turnovers, 2/7 FG, 2/4 3P, 1/3 FT, +3

Jaquez ended his streak of elite performances with this stinker. He made some solid plays here and there, but man, some of those turnovers were backbreaking. felt like the Bucks went on multiple runs that ended with deflating Jaquez giveaways.

22 minutes, 14 points, 6 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 turnovers, 5/11 FG, 3/6 3P, 0

Almost identical to the Celtics game, Kuzma started hot on 4/4 shooting, then made just one shot the rest of the way. Took two shots in the second half and had two turnovers before Jenkins took him out midway through the third and never put him back in.

23 minutes, 8 points, 7 rebounds, 1 block, 0 turnovers, 5 PF, 3/6 FG, 1/3 3P, -12

As I mentioned, the Hawks were switching everything with a bunch of like-sized players, and Turner has always struggled to play against switching defences because he can't punish mismatches. This basically rendered him obsolete. Suffice to say, a guy who is paid as much as Turner shouldn't be this easy to shut down.

24 minutes, 8 points, 11 rebounds, 2 assists, 3 blocks, 2/7 FG, 1/3 3P, 3/4 FT, +5

Even though he didn't score much, I liked Ware's motor, as shown by his block number and plus/minus. He continues to look more engaged on the defensive end and, at times, looked far and away the better option compared to Turner.

29 minutes, 13 points, 8 rebounds, 4 assists, 2 steals, 2 turnovers, 3/9 FG, 2/5 3P, 5/6 FT, -13

Burries found it tough to finish around the tall timber, but he was back to his do-everything ways and really made an impact on this game. Like Jakucionis, Burries' speed and physicality were needed against the up-and-in Hawks defence, and he rightly played a whole lot late because of that.

17 minutes, 5 points, 2 rebounds, 1 assist, 1 turnover, 2/5 FG, 1/3 3P, -9

30 minutes, 18 points, 2 rebounds, 3 steals, 7/16 FG, 4/12 3P, -3

We cool, Mr Silver? In all seriousness, Trent did provide a boost as a someone who was willing to get shots up at real volume once he got hot. But even more importantly, I just loved the energy he played with and how infectious he was out there. Anyone who has followed my writing knows how I feel about Trent's gambling defence (not a fan), but I guess when it comes off, he looks good.

11 minutes, 4 points, 2 rebounds, 2/3 FG, -4

Sims played only the opening five or so minutes of each half, but he was fine in those two spurts and did make an impact on the team's ability to compete for rebounds (even if I didn't love the combinations he was paired with). Made a nice floater off the reverse pivot in the first half.

Another surprise starter with Sims, and I can't say I loved how that unit played. In 10:50, the starting five had a -14.3 net rating. On the positive side, Jenkins clearly has a way of getting his groups to play with elite energy early in games, even if some of that has been driven by unsustainable shooting. Jenkins' MO to crash the glass was also a major reason they were hot early, outrebounding Atlanta 15-8 in the first quarter. On the note of unsustainable shooting, I also don't buy that it was Jenkins' fault that the team led by 22 and then was down two at the half; the shots the Bucks were making—and the Hawks were missing—just weren't going to continue. Finally, I liked how he kept cycling through units until he found something, even if that meant not playing Herro and Kuzma for the final quarter and a half.

Inactive: Kam Jones, Cormac Ryan, Pete Nance, Ousmane Dieng, Ryan Rollins, Bogoljub Markovic

If you play with energy and heart, Jenkins will reward you.

The Bucks shot a ridiculous 58% from the field and 55% from three in the first quarter. They actually did OK in some key metrics in the second quarter—even winning the possession battle 24-22—but their main issue was keeping the Hawks off the line; Atlanta shot 10 free throws to Milwaukee's one. The Bucks also turned it over eight times to the Hawks' three.

The Bucks got a season-high 62 points from their bench, outscoring the Hawks' bench by a whopping 28 points.

Gary Trent Jr. played his first first-quarter minutes all season, going 3/3 in the period.

Kyle Kuzma and Tyler Herro were subbed out in the middle of the third quarter and didn't return.

The Bucks have a few days to prepare for the big one against Giannis and the Miami Heat on Wednesday night in South Beach. Catch the Game on ESPN—yes, ESPN—at 6:00 p.m. CST.

#2671. Joe Burrow becomes the MVP favorite

Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow is having a potentially historic season. And, to no surprise, his performance has vaulted him past Bills quarterback Josh Allen as the favorite for the NFL MVP award.

After registering a fifth straight game with four or more total touchdowns — matching Peyton Manning (2004) as the only two players to ever do that — Burrow has surged to a +105 favorite to win the MVP trophy.

Along the way, the Bengals blasted the Steelers, 38-18. Burrow completed 35 of 44 passes for 409 yards and four touchdowns, as Cincinnati outgained Pittsburgh, 484 to 222.

Allen is second in the current odds, at +310. 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy lurks at +400, with Jaguars quarterback Trevor Lawrence at +500.

There's a gap after those four, with Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes at 16-1. (Seahawks receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who arguably best fits the official Associated Press definition of the term, remains an 80-1 long shot.)

The voting, which happens in the days after Week 18, will undoubtedly be influenced by the final configuration of the AFC and NFC playoff trees. Getting the top seed will give the quarterbacks of those teams a boost.

In the AFC, rhat could be the Bengals. Or the Bills. Or the Jaguars. Or the Chiefs. In the NFC, it could be the 49ers.

For now, Burrow has laid the foundation for a stretch run that earns his first career MVP award.

#2670. How much revenue Georgia athletics brought in for 2026 Sanford Stadium concert

The first Sanford Stadium concert in more than a decade last April tapped into a new revenue stream for Georgia athletics.

The "Live Between the Hedges," concert headlined by country stars Jason Aldean and Luke Bryan drew more than 60,000 fans to the football venue.

Georgia athletics made nearly $4.61 million in revenue, according to information provided to the Athens Banner-Herald under an open records request.

The school reported $4.035 million in ticket revenue, $460,429 in net concession sales and $111,102 in merchandise sales.

Georgia athletics' $4.61 million revenue figure is 50 percent of the total concert revenue. The show was put on in partnership with DOES Entertainment and Dugas-Jackson Consulting.

Georgia said the school also incurred expenses associated with the concert for such things as stage setup and concert staff.

The show, which also featured Zach Top and Lauren Alaina, on April 25 had gross concession sales of $1.85 million. That includes $1,489,968 in beer sales.

It was just the second concert in Sanford Stadium.

The first was also headlined by Bryan and Aldean and held in 2013.

"We have to continue to be creative in looking at different ways to drive revenue in more ways than ever before," athletic director Josh Brooks said in May of 2025.

The school is hosting three more concert dates in Sanford Stadium announced for 2027.

Singer-songwriter Noah Kahan will play on April 24 and country star Morgan Wallen on July 16 and 17.

This article originally appeared on Athens Banner-Herald: How much revenue Georgia athletics brought in for 2026 Sanford Stadium concert

#2668. Knicks 112, Raptors 108 (OT): “This was a low key huge win”

There aren't really many so-called "must-win games" during a basketball season. Technically, you only need to win elimination games, but the meaning of the term has broadened quite a bit over time and gets thrown around plenty over the course of the year for every team. Sometimes you even hear it after an early season contest, in a seemingly meaningless Sunday night—in a different country, to boot—and you wonder if we aren't getting ahead of ourselves here. We probably are, but no matter what, it sure beats the alternative: it's better to root for a team that we expect to win than one we expect to lose.

JA311 must have been mindful of this when he posted about the "low key huge win" in Russell's Postgame Thread, implying a reality that Knicks fans didn't want to inhabit this morning. It's a world where we would have had to accept that the shorthanded, slumping Raptors had snapped their 14-game losing-streak to our Knickerbockers, thus making the orange-and-blue ballers doubt their very existence.

If that were the case, New York would have fallen below .500 again after seemingly righting the ship against some Division-II level competition, only to crash back to earth when semi-competent NBA teams appeared before them. Yeah, luckily we don't have to deal with that feeling today and instead can bask in the glory of a hard-fought overtime victory on the road. Awesome, isn't it?

It would be even sweeter if, for the first forty minutes of the game, the Knicks hadn't put a serious scare in their faithful like a Michael Myers showing up at your front door on Halloween.

Some of the mistakes the team made last night put us at a loss for words, as when the easiest of passes rolled out of bounds, Austrian Jakob Poeltl skiied around them in the pick-and-roll as if he was Marcel Hirscher jetting down a slope, and Jamal Shead all of a sudden looked like the third Splash Brother. Sure, OG Anunoby was awesome in many facets of the game against his former team, but his dribble drives felt like you were watching your little one on a playground, climbing on a jungle gym that's only suited for much older kids. It feels like fingernails on a chalkboard sometimes and usually doesn't end well. Plus, in OG's case, I think we are beyond the "let him discover himself" phase.

Josh Hart was the hardest Knick to watch yesterday, and that is putting it mildly. Mike Brown certainly agreed, as Hart was pulled in the third quarter and never returned. The head coach probably also didn't like how the Dinos dominated the mismatch in the paint, which at times felt like the T-Rex dealing with that poor, sleazy lawyer in the first Jurrassic Park movie (Toronto, as has become a trend for New York, outscored the good guys 52-36 in the painted area). As the smallish Knicks were lured inside, more and more threes started falling on them like rain on a greyish Autumn day. But to say it with the words of Mr. Ian Malcolm: "Life, uh, finds a way." Or your beloved Knicks, for that matter.

Down 14 in the fourth quarter, the Knicks dug deep and found, among other things, James Wiseman (who was solid), their pride, and then that patented extra gear we've all grown accustomed to over the last 12 months. Karl-Anthony Towns dominated his matchup as he should, the defense buckled down (helped by a strong showing of Mikal Bridges out of all people), and Landry Shamet screamed: "I made fire". Jalen Brunson, indifferent for most of the night, rose to the occasion and made big-time decision after big-time decision. You miss the word shot here? That's the amazing part of Brunson's late-game heroics yesterday, as he first made his biggest impact by using his gravity to free up everyone around him. Of course, the captain wouldn't be the captain if he hadn't had a few massive jumpers himself, the biggest one being a tie-breaking dagger from the left corner in overtime.

That the comeback Knicks even needed overtime can be attributed to some out-of-body shooting luck by Scottie Barnes (who we all respect and wish well, but come on) and a debatable strategic decision by Mike Brown. I can understand him putting OG on former Knick Immanuel Quickley for the final possession, as nobody would have expected Barnes and his 20-something-percent downtown average to take the last top-of-the-key jumper. He certainly did, though, but luckily we got a replay a few minutes later with Anunoby defending the big Raptors forward this time around. It ended as it should – Barnes barely clanked the tying jumper off the backboard, and the oversized lady cleared her throat. Seconds later the Knicks were 7-6, with plenty to think about but also with a lot to be proud of. Among other things, there's the never-say-die attitude, their calmness in tight situations, a knack for role players to show up on any given night looking anything but.

And then there is the quality of pulling out a must-win game that really wasn't one. Or maybe it was? We'll see down the line, I guess.

#2667. Jaden McDaniels On Pace for Career Year with Minnesota Timberwolves

Nearly a month into the NBA season, teams across the league have begun to settle in as the quarter mark of the 82-game gauntlet approaches. Among the long list of contenders aiming for a deep run in 2026 is the Minnesota Timberwolves, which boasts one of the association's most daunting defensive units after restocking on elite talent over the offseason.

At the forefront of the stout group is former Washington Huskies star Jaden McDaniels.

In his seventh year in the Twin Cities, the veteran forward is off to a red-hot start. Through twelve games, the former Washington standout is shooting an impressive 51 percent from the field along with an average of 6 rebounds and 3 assists per outing, all of which would be career highs if he were to keep pace for the remainder of the season. While his offensive efficiency has seen a nice bump, his defensive impact is what makes the former Husky such an X-factor for head coach Chris Finch.

Through the early goings of the season, the T-Wolves sit atop the NBA in defensive rating, allowing just 103.8 points per 100 possessions. The high-end production stems from a trio of active defenders who also rank in the top 15 individually in the respective statistic (minimum 10 games): McDaniels (No. 12), guard LaMelo Ball (No. 5), and center Rudy Gobert (No. 4).

Since superstar Anthony Edwards went down in the first week of the season, Minnesota has managed to be just fine without the four-time All-Star. The team has won six of its last eight and is riding a five-game winning streak in the midst of an eight-game home stand. With Edwards out, McDaniels has been the primary defender against the opposition's top scorer, defending the likes of Cooper Flagg and Keyonte George in recent outings.

The defensive prowess should not come as a surprise, as the 6-foot-9, 185-pound forward has established himself as one of the top defenders in the league since being drafted in the first round in 2020. However, his presence on the offensive side of the ball has been a pleasant surprise, especially in the absence of Edwards.

The man they call "Slim" has posted ten or more points in every game this season, tied for the longest streak of anyone in the league. So far, McDaniels is averaging 16.9 points per game, which is a five-point jump from his career average.

As the two-way force continues to shine through the first month of the season, Minnesota will look to stay hot without their franchise cornerstone, who is expected to miss another 1-2 months. Fortunately, McDaniels and friends have looked to be just fine when it comes to making up for the production of Edwards, especially on the defensive end of the floor.

This article originally appeared on Huskies Wire: Jaden McDaniels On Pace for Career Year with Minnesota Timberwolves

#2666. 2026-27 NBA Power Rankings Week 5: Spurs move into top spot, focus on Number to Know

Welcome to the latest edition of the weekly NBC Sports NBA Power Rankings, where teams that are on 12-game win streaks and have Victor Wembanyama get to move to the front of the line. This week, we focus on numbers to know for each team.

Record: 12-2Ranking last week: No. 2Games this week: Detroit (on NBC), LA Clippers, New Orleans

Number to Know: San Antonio has a net rating of +12.6, just off Oklahoma City's historic rating (+12.7) in 2024-25 season, when the Thunder won 68 games and the NBA title. The Spurs are looking to become the first team to lose in the NBA Finals and then return to that big stage since the Cavaliers in 2018 — and they are off to a fast start. San Antonio has a top-three offensive and defensive rating. A lot of that has been because of Victor Wembanyama's impressive start to the season, but the guard lineups — with De'Aaron Fox, Dylan Harper, Stephon Castle and Devin Vassell, in whatever combination — are thriving as well. Check them out for yourselves Tuesday night on Coast 2 Coast on NBC and Peacock, starting at 8 ET.

Record: 11-2Ranking last week: No. 4Games this week: Orlando, at Denver, at Sacramento, at Golden State

Number to Know: The Boston Celtics are forcing 16.7 turnovers a game. Boston, under Joe Mazzulla, wasn't a team that forced many turnovers — until this season. The Celtics are forcing 4.3 more turnovers a game this season than a season ago as Mazzulla has adjusted his defensive philosophy (based on personnel) and it's working. Boston's win over Philadelphia last week was a reminder that if Paul George is healthy come April, the Celtics will be a very tough out.

Record: 12-2Ranking last week: No. 3Games this week: Charlotte, Utah, Sacramento

Number to Know: The Lakers have a -11.6 net rating when Luka Doncic is off the court. Luka Doncic is playing at an MVP level to start the season and is must-watch television — including Tuesday Night on NBC and Peacock this week when the Lakers host the Hornets. But the non-Luka minutes remain a concern, and they still have a -6.4 net rating when Doncic is off the court and Reaves is on. Doncic's incredible play and the Lakers' offense will make you forget all this. For now.

Record: 9-4Ranking last week: No. 6Games this week: Portland, Portland, New York, Memphis

Number to Know: Minnesota has the No. 1-ranked defense in the NBA, with a 104.5 defensive rating. After the Timberwolves front office reshaped the roster this summer, the expectation was that the defense would suffer, especially with the addition of LaMelo Ball. Not so fast, my friend — Ball is putting in the effort on defense, and Chris Finch has the right system around him with bigs protecting the paint. Minnesota is doing this without Anthony Edwards, a very strong perimeter defender in his own right. Rudy Gobert and Jaden McDaniels will get the headlines, but this has been a team effort.

Record: 11-3Ranking last week: No. 8Games this week: at Miami, at Indiana, at Denver

Number to Know: Jabari Smith Jr. is shooting 45% from the field, 38.6% from 3, and 85.7% from the free-throw line. He has been one of the unsung stars of the Rockets, hitting his open shots, and before the last two games I would have said Smith is in the running for a 50/40/90 season. Then he shot 5-of-24 over the past two games (including 2-of-12 from 3), and his season stats fell off. Still, he has benefited greatly from the improved spacing in Houston and has thrived this season. He is one reason the Rockets look like a threat.

Record: 11-3Ranking last week: No. 1Games this week: at Brooklyn, at Orlando, Milwaukee

Number to Know: Philadelphia is 9-0 in clutch games with a +43.6 net rating in those minutes. That clutch play is why the 76ers have the record they do and are ranked so highly. Philadelphia's +2 net rating for the season suggests a team that should be more like 7-6, but with LeBron James leading the way, this team wins its close games. If you're looking for a reason for the lower net rating, it's the pedestrian offense (18th in the league), but it was always going to take time to blend all those on-ball stars into a whole.

Record: 8-4Ranking last week: No. 7Games this week: at San Antonio, at New Orleans, Toronto, at Atlanta

Number to Know: Detroit has a -11.7 net rating in clutch minutes. There is some serious small sample size at play here as they have played in just five clutch games (within 5 points in the final five minutes), and the numbers look a lot better after Cade Cunningham's epic 52-point night in the double overtime win this week against the Wizards. However, overall, this low number speaks to the concern from last year's playoff run, when defenses loaded up on Cunningham and the team didn't have other good options. What helps is that their one option is elite.

Record: 9-3Ranking last week: No. 11Games this week: at Minnesota, at Minnesota, at Milwaukee, at New York

Number to Know: Portland has the best clutch net rating in the league at +55.3. This is some small sample size theater, the Trail Blazers have played in just five clutch games (inside 5 points in the final five minutes), but it doesn't feel like a coincidence that Damian Lillard returns and the Trail Blazers are winning close games. "Obviously, the closing of games, that's what this team struggled with last year," Coach Micha Nori said this week. "But that's where the effect of Dame coming back, the effect of calming. Deni (Avdija) is getting better in those situations, and the calming of Jrue (Holiday) and obviously Toumani's (Camara) defense."

Record: 7-4Ranking last week: No. 15Games this week: Phoenix, Boston, Houston, at Chicago

Number to Know: Aaron Gordon is shooting under 40% (39.8%) from the field and 27.3% on 3-pointers this season. Is this just a slow start to a season and nothing to worry about, or are these signs of Father Time and a lot of leg injuries catching up with him? Shot diet may have a lot to do with this, Gordon is taking a career-high 44.9% of his shot attempts from 3-point range and is averaging less than one dunk per game (the lowest in his career). Of course, this is the NBA, so some struggles leads to trade speculation, but Gordon is a Jokic favorite, so it would take a real haul in return for that to happen.

Record: 9-4Ranking last week: No. 14Games this week: at Washington, at Cleveland, Golden State, at Minnesota

Number to Know: The Grizzlies have a top-eight offense and defense in the league right now. Being in the top 10 in both is traditionally a sign of a contender (the Spurs, Celtics, Rockets and Timberwolves are the other teams doing it so far). However, with the Grizzlies the number feels inflated thanks to the hot start (6-0) and the easiest schedule in the league so far. Still, Memphis is beating the teams in front of them, which is all they can do.

Record: 7-6Ranking last week: No. 10Games this week: at Toronto, at Minnesota, Portland, Indiana

Number to Know: Josh Hart has gone scoreless in consecutive games, shooting 0-of-9 from the field in nearly 50 minutes of action. One of the stars of the Knicks' title run is off to a rough opening to this season, shooting 36.2% overall and 29.5% from 3. He's Josh Hart, so he gets a lot of rope, but is there cause for concern? Coach Mike Brown doesn't think so: "Josh is a pro. And he's been in this league long enough to understand what he needs to do to continue to get himself back on track because, at the end of the day, we need him. And he's a big part of what we do on both ends of the floor. And everybody knows that. And it's only a matter of time before he works his way out of it."

Record: 8-5Ranking last week: No. 5Games this week: Atlanta, New Orleans, at Miami

Number to Know: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander has shot 4-of-15 (26.7%) in the clutch this season. SGA is the reigning Clutch Player of the Year but this season he has struggled in the big moments. Part of that is the small sample size (just four games, the Thunder are 2-2 in those), and part of it is that Jalen Williams's injury (among others) allows defenses to focus more on SGA in those minutes. That was also the case for much of last season and he overcame it, nobody is actually worried about him, but it's a slow start.

Record: 8-5Ranking last week: No. 9Games this week: at New Orleans, at Dallas, at Memphis, Boston

Number to Know: The Warriors have a -0.7 net rating when Stephen Curry is off the court. Non-Curry minutes have long been an issue for the Warriors, but while he was healthy this season, Yaxel Landeborg and others stepped up and took over the offense while Curry rested. However, the Warriors have a -21.9 net rating in the past two games, the one where Curry got injured and the one where he did not suit up (abdominal injury that could have him out a month). It's going to be a rough few weeks in the Bay Area.

Record: 7-6Ranking last week: No. 19Games this week: Houston, Milwaukee, Oklahoma City

Number to Know: Miami has a -5.9 net rating in the third quarter this season. It was one of the things that stood out early in the season as the Heat stumbled out of the gate — they got blown out in the third quarter. That started to change recently, particularly when they put up 35 points on the Pistons in the third, in what the Heat feel like was a statement win last week. We'll see if this is a trend this week, with games against the Rockets and Thunder testing the Heat.

Record: 8-6Ranking last week: No. 16Games this week: at Oklahoma City, Charlotte, Detroit

Number to Know: Rookie Kingston Flemmings is finding his footing as a starter, averaging 8.6 points and 3.2 assists per game while shooting 56.3% in that role. Quin Snyder moved Flemmings into the starting lineup and he responded by scoring more, his usage rate went down but his efficiency went up, and the Hawks went 3-2 (he did not play Sunday vs. Milwaukee due to a lumbar strain). Snyder needs to find a way to keep either Fleming or Jalen Johnson on the court for most of the game.

Record: 7-7Ranking last week: No. 12Games this week: Chicago, Memphis, Indiana

Number to Know: James Harden is shooting just 39% this season. There is no single factor behind the Cavaliers' malaise at the start of the season, they have been pedestrian on offense and defense. However, James Harden has to play better — and he did against the Knicks, dropping 32 points and helping secure the win. Then two nights later, he was 5-of-13 shooting in a loss to the Heat.

Record: 7-7Ranking last week: No. 17Games this week: Golden State, LA Clippers, at Utah

Number to Know: Cooper Flagg has more 40+ point games than any teenager in NBA history, and this past week passed Kobe Bryant for second-most total points scored by a teenager. It's hard to overstate just how good Flagg has been in his second season, he has looked every bit an All-NBA player — and he doesn't turn 20 for a month. There are things to watch, such as Flagg shooting 26.8% on 3-pointers, but that should come around (he shot well in high school and college, his form is good, it just hasn't translated to the NBA yet), but overall this season could not have started better for the Mavericks' young star.

Record: 5-7Ranking last week: No. 22Games this week: at Denver, at Sacramento, at Utah

Number to Know: Phoenix is taking 19.6% of its shots at the rim, which ranks 25th in the league. Phoenix wasn't getting to the rim last season, either, taking 19.8% of its shots there (27th in the league) but the offseason additions of Jalen Green and Miles Bridges were supposed to change that. Instead, Suns fans are heading to the trade machines to come up with ways to get those two out of town. The Suns have 6-of-7 on the road starting Monday.

Record: 5-7Ranking last week: No. 23Games this week: at Boston, Philadelphia, at Brooklyn, at Washington

Stat of Note: Orlando's 109.7 offensive rating is 4.5 points per 100 possessions worse than it was a season ago. Chalk some of that up to injuries — Paolo Banchero remains out, Jalen Suggs just returned last week, Anthony Black missed time — but even so, this team still just does not seem to click on offense, and so far in this young season new coach Sean Sweeney hasn't been able to change that. Orlando's offense — and everything — looked better racking up wins against soft competition last week, that changes this week.

Record: 5-8Ranking last week: No. 13Games this week: New York, Washington, at Detroit

Number to Know: Toronto has the best fourth quarter net rating in the league at +16.6. Watch a lot of Raptors games and the pattern is obvious. They usually get an early lead, play the first half pretty even, struggle in the third quarter then try to come back in the fourth. That doesn't get a team consistent wins in the NBA. At least Scottie Barnes is healthy and back in the rotation after missing four games.

Record: 5-9Ranking last week: No. 20Games this week: Houston, at Cleveland, at New York

Number to Know: Indiana has a -4 net rating when Tyrese Haliburton is not on the court. It feels a little bit lazy to go to this stat, especially after a week when the Pacers picked up a quality NBA Cup win against the Knicks, but this remains the statistic that defines the Pacers' season. With Haliburton on the court, this is a dangerous team, without him they are inconsistent.

Record: 3-9Ranking last week: No. 26Games this week: Philadelphia, Chicago, Orlando

Number to Know: Jordi Fernandez is trying a super-big starting lineup — every player is 6'8" and up — and bringing his smaller young guards off the bench, to mixed success. For the past two games, the Nets starting five has been Egor Demin, Michael Porter Jr., Julius Randle, Danny Wolf and Day'Ron Sharpe, and in very limited minutes, it has a -2.7 net rating, and the team is 1-1. At this point, Fernandez should be throwing everything against the wall to see what sticks.

Record: 4-8Ranking last week: No. 25Games this week: Utah, at San Antonio, at Dallas

Number to Know: The Clippers are hitting 39.1% of their 3-pointers this season, the third-highest percentage in the league. LA doesn't take an extraordinary number of 3s (36.8 per game, 18th in the league), and it doesn't seem totally sustainable with Derrick Jones Jr. shooting 52.2% this season and Kris Dunn at 40%, but it's working for the Clippers so far.

Record: 4-10Ranking last week: No. 18Games this week: Memphis, at Toronto, at Chicago, Orlando

Number to Know: AJ Dybantsa is averaging 15.1 points and 6.2 rebounds per game. Wizards ownership/management wanted to win now and went out and got Trae Young (and gave him an oversized extension) and Anthony Davis, but Dybantsa is showing he is clearly the future. The Wizards need to focus on him and his timeline, and just give him the rock more.

Record: 4-9Ranking last week: No. 24Games this week: at Los Angeles Lakers, at Atlanta

Number to Know: The Charlotte Hornets have the worst offense in the NBA this season with a 102.5 offensive rating. Or, look at it this way: Charlotte is the only team in the league not averaging 100 points per game. Injuries have a lot to do with this, with Kon Knueppel missing time and Brandon Miller having just returned from missing a couple of games. That makes the second game on NBC's Coast to Coast Tuesday this week a real contrast, going up against the Lakers and the best offense in the NBA so far. Check the game out for yourself at 11 p.m. Eastern on NBC or Peacock.

Record: 3-9Ranking last week: No. 30Games this week: at Cleveland, at Brooklyn, Washington, Denver

Number to Know: Caleb Wilson is averaging 18.9 points and 6.2 rebounds per game. Which is really just a stat I'm using to say how much it sucks that a hand fracture is keeping him out for 4- 6 weeks. It's not that the Bulls are better or worse with him on the court — they have been equally bad whether he was playing or not — but it sucks for Bulls fans and is one less reason to tune in and watch this team.

Record: 4-10Ranking last week: No. 21Games this week: Golden State, Detroit, at Oklahoma City, at San Antonio

Number to Know: Jeremiah Fears is averaging 15.3 points, 5.2 assists and 4.5 rebounds a game this season. This is worth noting because he is clearly the point guard of the future, especially since Dejounte Murray wants to be traded, his agent (Rich Paul of Klutch Sports) told the team last week. Fears has work to do on his 3-point shot and efficiency, but toss the man the keys and let him drive the car and learn.

Record: 1-11Ranking last week: No. 28Games this week: Phoenix, at Los Angeles Lakers, Boston

Number to Know: Domantas Sabonis is averaging 14.2 points per game to start the season. As always with Sabonis, look at just the counting stats and it's not terrible — a double-double with 13.2 rebounds a game, shooting 63.8% — but watch him on the court while Darius Acuff Jr. takes over and it seems his mind is on Grand Theft Auto 6 (or somewhere else). Yes, the Kings are willing to trade Sabonis, but his contract means that is more likely a move next summer.

Record: 1-12Ranking last week: No. 27Games this week: at LA Clippers, at Los Angeles Lakers, Phoenix, Dallas

Number to Know: The Utah Jazz are already 5.5 games back of the final play-in spot in the West. The Jazz have lost 12 in a row, but give them credit for playing hard, as they did to push the Spurs (a little) on Sunday. Utah has been the most disappointing team in the NBA this season. This was the year they were going to turn things around, be competitive, make the playoffs, and instead fit and injury issues have derailed this team. It's just hard to find the positives right now.

Record: 1-13Ranking last week: No. 29Games this week: at Miami, Portland, at Philadelphia

Number to Know: The Bucks are bottom six in the league in three of the offensive four factors (that are the baseline of analytics): eFG% (50.9), free throw rate (23.8), and turnover percentage (16.7). At least they are pretty good on the offensive glass. It's hard to come up with positives, but Kasparas Jakucionis dropped 25 on the Hawks Sunday, he's been inconsistent this season but maybe he deserves more of a chance. What else is Taylor Jenkins going to do?

#2665. Gila, ex Lazio: «Grazie allo psicologo ho cambiato prospettiva»

Dopo un periodo difficile all’inizio della carriera in Italia, il difensore dice di affrontare gli errori con più serenità.

Mario Gila, ex Lazio oggi al Milan, ha raccontato di essersi rivolto a uno psicologo dopo un periodo difficile vissuto all’inizio della carriera in Italia. Il difensore ne ha parlato nel podcast The Chamber, nell’ambito di un’iniziativa rossonera dedicata al benessere mentale.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Gila ha descritto le pressioni di un mestiere che, visto dall’esterno, può far apparire un calciatore di Serie A come una persona privilegiata e con pochi problemi personali. Nella sua esperienza, invece, il lavoro richiede un impegno mentale continuo, dentro e fuori dal campo.

«Un calciatore tende sempre ad avere la mente attiva. È una professione che comporta un grande dispendio di energie mentali», ha spiegato Gila. Per questo cerca occasioni in cui entrare in contatto con se stesso e ritrovare quel Mario che, a volte, sente di perdere a causa del lavoro.

Il difensore ritiene che la professione possa allontanare i giocatori da se stessi, anche per le situazioni da gestire fuori dal campo. Alimentazione, preparazione atletica e allenamenti scandiscono la vita quotidiana: da calciatori, ha osservato, si resta tali ventiquattr’ore su ventiquattro. Tutto va tenuto sotto controllo per arrivare al fine settimana nelle migliori condizioni.

Gila ha parlato anche del peso della ricerca della perfezione: «La perfezione ti sfinisce, è estenuante, e credo anche noiosa fino a un certo punto». Secondo lui, inseguirla può impedire di vedere fino in fondo l’essenza autentica di una persona. Per molto tempo ha adottato quell’atteggiamento; ora prova ad accettare maggiormente gli altri per come sono e a comprenderne il momento.

Ripensando all’inizio della carriera in Italia, Gila ha detto di avere attraversato una fase dura e di aver toccato il fondo. «Grazie a uno psicologo sono riuscito a superarlo», ha raccontato. Prima era molto severo con se stesso: non si concedeva di sbagliare e, quando accadeva, si giudicava negativamente.

Oggi considera l’errore parte del mestiere e un’occasione per migliorare e crescere. Dice di affrontarlo con più serenità e di riuscire a elaborarlo meglio, senza rinunciare a cercare una soluzione, tanto sul piano professionale quanto su quello privato. Guardare una situazione negativa da una prospettiva positiva, ha spiegato, cambia il modo in cui vive ciò che è accaduto: il rumore che accompagnava l’errore lascia spazio alla calma.

Per Gila è normale commettere lo stesso sbaglio più di una volta. In quei momenti ritiene più utile trattarsi con gentilezza e capire che cosa sia successo, anziché lasciarsi trascinare dalla negatività. L’obiettivo, nelle sue parole, è cercare di sentirsi in pace.

#2664. VOTE: CFBHN/Herald-Tribune Boys Athlete of the Week for Nov. 9-14

Each week, the Herald-Tribune staff will select nominees for the Herald-Tribune Boys Athlete of the Week poll sponsored by Central Florida Behavioral Network, Inc. Nominees are derived from scores and stats emailed in by Sarasota and Manatee County coaches during the week to htincoming@gmail.com. Readers can then vote in the online poll to determine the Boys Athlete of the Week.

The Herald-Tribune Boys Athlete of the Week sponsored by Central Florida Behavioral Health Network for Nov. 2-7, 2026, was Manatee golfer Ty Wailand, who won the poll with 54.8 percent of the vote. Wailand tied for eighth in Region 3A-3, shooting a 76.

A poll will be posted at heraldtribune.com each Monday, and voting will end at 10 a.m. Friday each week.

The nominees for the week of Nov. 9-14, 2026 are:

Chase Marshall, Wellen Park: Marshall finished 10th for Wellen Park in the Region 2A-3 meet, running a 17:22.7. Marshall helped the Eagles to a fifth place finish.

Gabe Milliken, Sarasota Christian: Milliken won the Region 1A-3 title, running a 16:48.8.

Davin Davidson, Cardinal Mooney: In nine minutes of work, Davidson finished 10-of-11 for 103 yards and three touchdowns in Mooney's 49-0 win over Dunedin in the 3A-3 regional quarterfinal.

Trenton Huffman, Riverview: Huffman had two touchdowns and 76 receiving yards behind five receptions in Riverview's 52-28 win over Haines City in the 6A-3 regional quarterfinal.

Steven LeBlanc, Saint Stephen's: LeBlanc scored the game-winning touchdown that propelled Saint Stephen's to an 18-14 win over Oxbridge Academy to advance to the SSAA Bound Championship.

Freedom McDaniel, Braden River: McDaniel scored the game-winning touchdown in Braden River's 17-14 win over Jefferson in the 3A-3 regional quarterfinal. McDaniel also recovered a fumble at the Braden River 1-yard line to stop Jefferson. He also blocked a 26-yard field goal in the third quarter and recorded a sack in the fourth.

Nazir Pitchford, Palmetto: Pitchford had an pick-six late in the third quarter, helping Palmetto take a 17-7 lead that led to an eventual 23-7 victory over Royal Palm Beach in the 5A-3 regional quarterfinal.

Kymani Sellers, Palmetto: Sellers had five tackles, two tackles for loss, one sack and four quarterback pressures in Palmetto's 23-7 win over Royal Palm Beach in the 5A-3 regional quarterfinal.

Kael Kohrman, Parrish Community: Kohrman scored twice in Parrish's 8-0 win over Armwood.

Miguel Lopez, Parrish Community: Lopez scored twice in Parrish's 8-0 win over Armwood.

#2663. Kasper feels hosting NFL game at Allianz Arena is "important" for Bayern's global growth

Rouven Kasper believes hosting tomorrow's NFL game where the New England Patriots face the Detroit Lions at the Allianz Arena will only grow Bayern Munich's international recognition.

“It is important for our internationalisation because the [NFL] teams train at our Campus and at Säbener Straße," Bayern's marketing director told BILD.

"There are a lot of cameras that naturally help us reach audiences in America as well. That gives exposure for Munich, for the city and for us as a club.

"We also produce a lot of content. A few weeks ago, Giovanni Elber was in Switzerland with an NFL legend, up on a high mountain, shooting some content.

“Those images are shared around the world, which is why this is very relevant to us strategically in terms of our internationalisation,” he explained.

#2662. Report: Brock Bowers is ‘day-to-day’

The Las Vegas Raiders were riding high after Fernando Mendoza's first touchdown. However, they received bad news after their first drive of the game.

Brock Bowers injured his ankle while blocking on a run play in the first quarter. They took him inside the tarp, and he returned briefly. After the touchdown, they took him to the locker room. Reports indicate he is questionable to return.

Times like this are why you paid Michael Mayer. He and Ian Thomas will have to step up and take over at tight end. Mendoza will have to lean on those two to make plays and other weapons on offense.

Hopefully it is not a serious injury for Bowers, as he is vital to the offense. He is the best tight end in football, and he will be missed if he can't go for now.

Update: Bowers has returned to the game after coming back from the locker room.

Now, Bowers went back to the locker room in the second quarter.

The Raiders ruled him out of the game at halftime.

Raiders' coach Klint Kubiak didn't have an update on Bowers after the game.

Monday, NFL Media reported Bowers did not suffer a major injury and he is "day-to-day." thus he may be able to play Sunday at Denver,

#2661. Huge TSSAA football playoff outbursts. Vote for Ponce Law Athlete of Week

The TSSAA football playoffs bring in a new batch of standout performances.

#2659. Parker Washington has been dynamic for Jaguars

If the NFL playoffs began right now, the Jacksonville Jaguars would host the Pittsburgh Steelers on Wild Card weekend.

As we noted during Week 9, the Jaguars should be considered among the league's elite teams. Jacksonville leads the NFL with a point differential of +125 (the San Francisco 49ers are second in the NFL with a differential of +85) and the Jaguars are in the top five in both Offensive and Defensive Expected Points Added per Play. Jacksonville has an Offensive EPA/Play of 0.125 (ranking them fourth behind San Francisco, Cincinnati, and Buffalo) and a Defensive EPA/Play of -0.103 (ranking them fourth behind Minnesota, Tampa Bay, and the Los Angeles Rams).

They are the only team in the top five in both categories.

General manager James Gladstone made some aggressive moves ahead of the trade deadline including adding safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis, but another key player for the Jaguars right now is wide receiver Parker Washington. Washington has grown into a reliable target for quarterback Trevor Lawrence in the passing game, and enjoyed a career outing against the Tennessee Titans, catching seven passes for 152 yards and a touchdown, as Jacksonville improved to 7-2 with a 40-23 win.

And Washington delivered some highlight-reel moments in the process.

His first catch of the game was actually his touchdown, which came on a slant route with the Jaguars knocking on the door of the end zone:

Washington's next reception came on a seam route, working against man coverage. Watch as he releases to the outside out of the left slot, avoids any jam from the defensive back, and makes a tough adjustment on a throw that is slightly behind him as well as high:

The receiver also showed his skills working along the sideline. ON this completion from late in the first quarter, Washington runs a deep out pattern. Lawrence makes this throw with pristine timing and anticipation, but the adjustment and body control Washington displays as he pulls the throw in and gets both feet down, are elite:

Then came this corner route late in the first half. Working against a two-deep coverage, Lawrence targets Washington on the corner route, squeezing in a throw between the half-field safety and the cornerback sinking under the deep route. While the Titans do what they can to try and take this route away, Washington simply wins at the catch point:

And yes, I have Gus Johnson saying "he goes up and … gets it" in my head every time I watch this clip.

But the play from Washington that had all of social media buzzing — and likely sent shivers down the spine of every defensive back in the league — was this catch early in the second quarter. Watch how Washington, working out of the left slot, puts Alontae Taylor in the spin cycle:

Now, I try and avoid "screenshot scouting" as much as possible but I have to ask: Is this good?

Washington initially starts by working across the field, and then takes a step vertically to flash a move to the outside. Taylor bites on that outside move and breaks toward the sideline, just as Washington continues across the field on his crossing route. This short throw, covering just six yards from the line of scrimmage to the catch point, ends up as a 50-yard gain.

Washington finished the game having caught seven passes for 152 yards — again, a career-high mark — and the touchdown.

Jacksonville's emergence as one of the AFC's elite teams is a huge storyline this season.

And Washington's emergence as a trusted target for Lawrence is a big part of that story.

#2657. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2656. Report: Aidan Hutchinson is out for the season with torn ACL, likely additional damage

Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson will miss the rest of the season with a serious knee injury he suffered while celebrating a sack on Sunday.

Hutchinson has a torn ACL in his right knee and probably additional damage, according to Ian Rapoport.

The torn ACL was seen on the MRI he had in Germany after leaving Sunday's game, and the team plans to give him additional tests now that he's back in Detroit. There are concerns that he also injured his meniscus.

Hutchinson is one of the best defensive players in the NFL and his loss is devastating to the Lions, who are 7-2 and have legitimate Super Bowl hopes. They also had legitimate Super Bowl hopes two years ago, when Hutchinson suffered a season-ending broken leg, and their defense wasn't the same without him.

The injury came moments after Hutchinson sacked Drake Maye. Hutchinson got up, jumped in the air celebrating, and landed awkwardly, with his right knee seeming to buckle. He immediately went to the ground and grabbed his leg.

Maye was also injured on the play, missed the rest of the game and is likely out for a significant period of time.

#2654. Eagles News: Patriots writer says A.J. Brown trade “keeps looking worse by the day”

Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation!

A.J. Brown looked really good for the Patriots against the Eagles in training camp. But he's been pretty bad since getting banged up in Week 1. He hasn't been able to get healthy and Pats fans seem to be wondering if he might be cooked at this point. Brown's 26 targets this season have resulted in just 11 receptions for 128 yards (11.6 average). As a reminder, the Eagles will receive the Patriots' 2027 fifth-round pick (which will become increasingly favorable for Philly as New England continues to lose) and their 2028 first-round pick from the Brown trade.

Let's get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links …

10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Lions – Pats Pulpit

The A.J. Brown trade keeps looking worse by the day. A.J. Brown's inability to do anything positive this year has been almost laughable. He got hurt in the first game, missed a good chunk of time on injured reserve, came back, was a non-factor, and then got hurt again. He returned on Sunday, was unable to get open and had a drop as well. He finally made a nice catch-and-run to move the stick on a third down, and then promptly went to the locker room with a hamstring injury. It's been a rough year for Brown, and the Patriots front office: they effectively bid against themselves to trade for him and still gave up a first-round pick in 2028 to do so. Unless he somehow manages a complete 180, the trade is going to go down as a massive failure, and potentially hamstring the Patriots for years to come.

Howie Roseman seen chatting up one of the top quarterback draft prospects – BGN

The Philadelphia Eagles are on their bye this weekend and Howie Roseman is spending part of the team's time off by attending Saturday's college football game between Duke and the University of Miami. This isn't necessarily a formal scouting trip for Roseman; his son, Jake, attends Duke and contributes to the Blue Devils' football program. The Eagles' general manager could be there to primarily spend time with family. That being said, it is interesting to see that Roseman was chatting it up with one of the top prospects in the 2027 NFL Draft. Here's a video of him meeting with Miami Hurricanes quarterback Darian Mensah during pregame warmups.

Eagles rookie progress reports, midway through the season – PhillyVoice

There have been a lot of excuses made for Makai Lemon's low impact rookie season, some of which are valid, in my opinion, but some of which are not. Certainly, he is playing in a non-functional offense getting targets from Tanner McKee and Joe Milton. That's valid. However, I've seen a number of Eagles fans cite a stat from PFF that says that Lemon has a high "separation percentage." If you've seen this stat and have been encouraged by it, I hate to yuck your yum but there may not be a more useless metric in the NFL statistical zeitgeist. Here were PFF's "separation percentage" leaders in 2025. It's a "who's who" of low impact receivers. I mean, JAHAN DOTSON (!) was in the top 10, lol. […] Lemon is not Jalen Reagor. But he is also not Amon-Ra St. Brown. If his drop issues are just a short-term rookie issue, then he can grow into a useful, gritty chain mover / frisky blocker from the slot in an efficient offense. However, I just don't see a lot of explosiveness, and I do think his ceiling is capped by the combination of that and his lack of size.

Examining Howie Roseman's Eagles bye week: From trading Jordan Davis to watching Miami-Duke – The Athletic

Moro Ojomo hasn't shown it with sacks this season — and the sacks need to come — but the advanced pass-rushing data is encouraging. He leads the Eagles with 16 hurries and is tied for a team-high with 21 pressures. His pressure rate of 9.6 percent is down from 11.6 percent last season and 12.2 percent in 2024, but it's still a strong rate for an interior rusher. His pressure rate and quarterback hit rate of 2.3 percent are both better than Carter and Davis. He also has the type of football character and work ethic worthy of an investment, and would fit on even fronts if the Eagles changed defensive schemes. The Eagles lost a respected locker-room figure with Davis' departure, but I'd feel comfortable entrusting Ojomo with a bigger presence. He's already called "Coach Mo" among the defensive linemen. The Eagles will have to pay a high price to keep him. It's the type of move Roseman should feel comfortable making. It might even take off some of the sting of losing Milton Williams two years ago.

NFL playoff chance tiers: Where all 32 teams fit in 2026 postseason picture – ESPN

Tier 8: Just rest up for 2027. Philadelphia Eagles (2-7). Chances to make the playoffs: 0.3%. Fret not, Eagles fans, because if there's one thing Philadelphia does better than any other team in the league, it's taking advantage of the opportunity a losing season provides. Recognizing that they had virtually no shot at the playoffs with quarterback Jalen Hurts out for the season, the Eagles made some amazing pre-deadline trades, somehow getting a second-round pick (plus a Day 3 pick swap!) for center Cam Jurgens and first- and second-round picks for Jordan Davis. So sure, 2026 is effectively over for the Eagles, but they set themselves up so well for 2027 and beyond.

Steelers stock report after 38-18 loss to the Bengals – Behind The Steel Curtain

Checking in on the Eagles' Week 11 opponent.

Offensive Firepower. Aaron Rodgers started this game 0/7 passing. Admittedly, it wasn't all his fault, which is why we will talk about the entire offense here. The Steelers' passing game is incredibly limited, and not really built to play against teams like Cincinnati that can light up the scoreboard. Their receivers struggle to separate, and that won't get better over the course of their last eight games. The Bengals were more than prepared for the Steelers' run game, which they didn't even try to establish until they were already down multiple scores. From the quarterback to the playmakers to the coaching, something is going to need to change drastically to take this team seriously against any quality competition.

#2652. Jahmyr or JSN: Who's the Offensive Player of the Year in the NFL this season?

Imagine you're an offensive coordinator in the NFL. And, as long as we're in the world of make-believe, imagine you have both Jahmyr Gibbs and Jaxon Smith-Njigba on your roster. And imagine you have exactly one play to get into the end zone.

Do you go with the running back who can stomp upstream through rush-hour traffic? Or do you go with the receiver who can create space in a mosh pit? Ground game or air game? Who's your favorite for NFL Offensive Player of the Year?

Sunday served as center stage for both Gibbs and Smith-Njigba, half a world apart. Before half the United States had even woken up, Gibbs began a methodical demolition of New England in Munich, rushing for 153 yards and two touchdowns and receiving another 99 through the air as Detroit won 35-10. A few hours later, Smith-Njigba caught eight passes for 171 yards, including a 71-yard beast of a touchdown, as Seattle outlasted Las Vegas 21-13.

Through Week 10, both teams remain in the hunt for playoff berths, in large part because of the outsized, generational performances of their stars.

After three seasons in the backfield alongside David Montgomery as a Sonic-and-Knuckles duo, Gibbs is now a solo act; Detroit thought enough of his potential that the Lions dealt Montgomery to the Texans. Gibbs validated the Lions' trust in him; this season, he leads the NFL in (deep breath) attempts, yards, touchdowns, first downs, rushing yards per game, touches from scrimmage, yards from scrimmage and combined receiving and rushing touchdowns.

Just three-plus seasons into his career, Gibbs is already starting to carve his way into the NFL record books. He just passed Terrell Davis for the most touchdowns through the first four years of a career, with 62. And he joined a couple guys named Emmitt Smith and Barry Sanders as the only players to rush for 50 touchdowns before turning 25.

"I think we have to pinch ourselves sometimes and not take for granted how special he is," Lions quarterback Jared Goff said after Sunday's victory. "He's just so explosive with the ball in his hands. I throw a check-down to him, and he goes for 50 yards. That's so rare for a guy to be able to do all the things he does."

Here, from Sunday, is a perfect encapsulation of everything Gibbs brings to the field: speed, power and a relentless drive into the end zone.

Also in his fourth year, Smith-Njigba is both a defending Super Bowl champion and the defending Offensive Player of the Year. While Seattle is struggling to defend its title, Smith-Njigba is authoring a brilliant sequel to his 2025. He currently leads the league in (another deep breath) receptions, receiving yards, receiving touchdowns, receiving first downs, longest reception, receiving yards per game and yards per touch from scrimmage.

His performance Sunday against the Raiders was nothing short of exceptional. He totaled 144 yards in a decisive third quarter, including that magnificent 71-yard touchdown … that came after he lost his footing starting his route.

"The thing that stuck out today was he's making [plays] in all phases of the game," Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald said after Sunday's game. "On the extended plays, he's able to uncover and go become a target for our quarterback as well. So it's really in every stage of how we're playing offense. So it's pretty remarkable. He's a beast."

The most impressive fact about Smith-Njigba's dominance is that everyone on the other side of the ball knows it's coming … and they still can't stop it. Seattle doesn't have any other true receiving threats on the roster; Cooper Kupp, the Seahawks' second-leading receiver, is nearly a thousand yards behind JSN's current total of 1,207.

The Offensive Player of the Year award now tends to reward non-quarterback skill players; the last QB to win was Patrick Mahomes in 2018. It's also an award with a wide pool of candidates; the last repeat winner was Marshall Faulk, who won the award three straight times from 1999 to 2001.

Back to the question at the top: You're that offensive coordinator blessed with more talent than any team should have. So who would you choose to score that one-play touchdown, Jahmyr Gibbs or Jaxon Smith-Njigba?

Brazil knocked out Japan from the World Cup with an injury-time strike, but the roles were reserved on Saturday when the two national teams met for a friendly game in Singapore. The Samurai Blue saw their two-goal lead canceled by a brace from Vinicius Junior before Tatsuhiro Sakamoto's first international goal in the 91st minute repeated the shoreline from last year's friendly in Tokyo.

Five Bundesliga-based players featured for Japan, who will go their separate ways with their iconic coach Hajime Moriyasu after Tuesday's game against Paraguay following the postponement of the Asian Cup. Eintracht Frankfurt's attacking midfielder Ritsu Doan captained the side once again, with Gladbach's Ko Itakura entering as a late substitute.

The 28-year-old assisted Takefusa Kubo's opening goal before Keito Nakamura doubled Japan's advantage inside the first twenty minutes. Tensions were raising after the winning goal for Japan as both Carlo Ancelotti and Raphinha saw red cards for their protests in the dugout.

Hoffenheim's Koki Machida and Bayern's Hiroki Ito started in defense for Japan, while Mainz's Kaishu Sano came off the bench like his brother who currently plays for Eredivisie leaders PSV. Japan will stay in Kallang for the game against Paraguay, where Brazil face Singapore for the very first time.

#2649. Three reasons why the Jaguars beat the Titans

The Jacksonville Jaguars are beginning to look like a serious problem for the rest of the AFC.

Liam Coen's side traveled to Nashville on Sunday and came away with a convincing 40-23 victory over the Tennessee Titans, extending their winning streak to three games and improving their record to 7-2. With the Houston Texans slipping up against Cleveland, Jacksonville now holds a commanding four-game advantage at the top of the AFC South.

There were plenty of positives for the visitors, but this wasn't simply a case of taking advantage of a struggling divisional rival. The Jaguars demonstrated why they are becoming one of the most dangerous teams in the conference.

Here are three reasons why Jacksonville came away with the victory.

There have been plenty of questions about Trevor Lawrence throughout his NFL career. Is he capable of being the franchise quarterback Jacksonville hoped they were getting when they selected him first overall in 2021? Can he consistently deliver the performances expected of a quarterback of his considerable talent?

Right now, those questions are looking increasingly redundant.

Lawrence was outstanding against Tennessee, completing 23 of 35 passes for 352 yards and three touchdowns. He connected with nine different receivers, demonstrating the sort of command and confidence that makes this Jacksonville offense so difficult to defend.

Perhaps most encouragingly, this wasn't an isolated performance. Lawrence has now surpassed 300 passing yards in three of his last five games, while the Jaguars have scored at least 30 points in four consecutive outings.

The connection between Lawrence and head coach Liam Coen is becoming increasingly apparent. The quarterback looks comfortable in the offensive system, understands where his opportunities are coming from, and is playing with the sort of conviction that can elevate an entire offense.

Lawrence also reached 20,000 career passing yards against Tennessee, becoming the eighth-youngest player in NFL history to achieve the milestone.

Jacksonville has a quarterback playing with genuine confidence, and that could make the Jaguars a very difficult proposition come January.

Trevor Lawrence deserves plenty of the credit, but he also needs players capable of turning opportunities into big plays. Against Tennessee, Parker Washington provided exactly that.

The young receiver enjoyed a spectacular afternoon, finishing with 152 receiving yards and a touchdown. Remarkably, he had already accumulated 148 yards by halftime, giving the Titans defense all sorts of problems before the interval.

Washington's ability to create separation and generate yards after the catch gives Jacksonville another dimension in the passing game. He isn't simply a possession receiver waiting for the ball to come to him; he is capable of turning relatively routine completions into substantial gains.

His performance also highlights an important development in Jacksonville's offense. Lawrence isn't reliant on one individual to produce. Washington, Brenton Strange, and Josh Cameron all found the end zone, while nine different receivers caught passes.

That variety makes life considerably harder for opposing defensive coordinators. Concentrate too heavily on one threat and another player is likely to make you pay.

With Washington producing performances like this, Jacksonville has another weapon capable of making a significant difference down the stretch.

There is no getting away from the fact that Tennessee's defense had a miserable afternoon.

Jacksonville finished with 459 total yards, averaged 6.4 yards per play, and converted seven of its 14 third-down opportunities. The Jaguars also controlled possession for more than 38 minutes, leaving the Titans with precious little opportunity to build any sustained momentum.

It wasn't just Lawrence's passing that caused problems, either. Jacksonville accumulated 123 rushing yards, with Bhayshul Tuten adding a late six-yard touchdown to put the finishing touches on the victory.

The inability to get off the field was particularly damaging. Jacksonville repeatedly extended drives, controlled the tempo, and forced Tennessee's defense to spend long periods chasing the game.

There were mitigating circumstances for Robert Saleh. Tennessee has undergone significant personnel changes, with injuries and trades leaving the defensive unit considerably depleted. But the numbers make for uncomfortable reading regardless.

Giving up 40 points and 459 yards is not a recipe for success against an offense with the talent Jacksonville possesses.

The Titans managed to stay within touching distance for much of the contest, but their inability to consistently disrupt Lawrence and get the ball back to their own offense ultimately proved costly.

There is still plenty of football to be played, but Jacksonville is putting together an impressive body of work.

Lawrence is playing with confidence, the receiving corps is developing into a dangerous group, and Coen's offense is producing points consistently.

The Jaguars weren't perfect against Tennessee, and there are defensive areas they will want to address, but winning on the road by 17 points against a divisional opponent is exactly the sort of business a playoff contender should be taking care of.

At 7-2, with a four-game lead in the AFC South, Jacksonville has given itself an excellent platform for the second half of the season.

The question is no longer whether the Jaguars can win their division. It's how far this team can go once the playoffs arrive.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.
