#2643. Chiefs Week 10 snap count analysis: Ashton Gillotte does it all

Welcome to Arrowhead Pride's weekly snap-count analysis!

Let's take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs' snap counts in the 35-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus' premium stats.

Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Joshua Ezeudu, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Rashee Rice, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Noah Gray and TE Travis Kelce

Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, NT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, LB Jack Cochrane, CB Nohl Williams, CB Mansoor Delane, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner

Inactive: QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), RB Kenneth Walker (groin), FB Ben VanSumeren, RB Jaydn Ott (hamstring), DT Peter Woods (neck), CB Melvin Smith Jr. and RT Jaylon Moore (ankle)

As the season has worn on, defensive end Ashton Gillotte has become an increasingly important part of the defense. He started the season recovering from a plantar fascia injury, and now he's one of the most versatile players in the defense's front seven.

He has played two-thirds of the defense's snaps in each of the last three weeks; in Atlanta, he was on the field for 75% of the time the defense was.

He didn't start against the Falcons, but he racked up five tackles, one sack, two tackles for loss and a pass broken up. Pro Football Focus credited Gillotte with six pressures total and led all Chiefs defenders in "Stops" (4), tackles that constitute a failure for the offense.

He made a big impact while lining up in the B-gap 31 of the 52 times he was on the field; most of that time, he rushed the passer from the inside. He also lined up as an off-ball linebacker on two snaps, giving the Chiefs a unique run-defense look in their base 4-3 formation alongside linebackers Nick Bolton and Drue Tranquill.

In his Chiefs debut, new receiver Josh Downs lined up for just 10 snaps and ran eight routes, totaling 51 yards and a touchdown over four catches.

It was clear that Downs will be a key part of the passing game moving forward, so whose snaps are going to be reduced to make room for Downs in future weeks?

Worthy is the easy answer here, because it's incredible how little production comes out of leading the receiver room in snaps each week. In Atlanta, he was targeted three times, and none were completed.

Rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas played 48 snaps in Atlanta, the second-most snaps in his career. However, Thomas did not register a quarterback pressure over the 39 pass-rush snaps; it's the first time he was held without a pressure this season.

Despite the Chiefs playing with a lead and giving Thomas plenty of opportunity to rush the passer, his impact was not felt. Kansas City generated plenty of pressure, but none came from Thomas, a recent trend: the rookie has only two pressures over the last three games.

In the three games between Weeks 4-7, Thomas racked up 14 pressures — but hasn't reached the same level of impact since.

#2641. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2640. Seahawks post-game droppings: Raiders first-round treasure sunk by Seahawks defense

Let that relaxation set in for the next two weeks as the Seattle Seahawks head into their bye on a two-game winning streak after coming alive in the second half in a 21-13 win over the Las Vegas Raiders. It was one of those "get it done any way you can" games, with injuries piling up for Seattle. On the other side of the field was the No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza making his first start at quarterback, leading to a suddenly hot ticket in Sin City. Despite more injuries, turnovers, and a missed FG, Seattle found a way to get the win and now get a few weeks to regroup for the stretch run of the season.

Seattle's defense started slow, then exploded. One would think that Mike Macdonald's defense facing a rookie QB in his first start would mean a very rough day for Mendoza. It didn't start out that way with two straight scoring drives given up by the Seahawks. Mendoza got the ball out quickly and accurately, and used his legs when needed to extend plays and get into the endzone. After those early drives, the Seahawks defense CLAMPED DOWN. At one point in the fourth quarter, the Raiders had -17 yards of offense in the second half. A stupid 38-yard pass play from Mendoza to Jeanty near the end of the fourth quarter bumped the numbers up for Mendoza, but he still finished with just 143 passing yards. The Seahawks sacked him six times for a staggering 45 yards lost! They also held the Raiders to 65 yards rushing for the game. That equates to 163 total yards for the suffocating Seattle defense. They didn't force any turnovers, but the Raiders had nowhere to go after those first two drives.

Seattle's offense started slow, then exploded…mostly in the third quarter. Drew Lock was back in at QB, and Seattle had its one-two punch of Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price at their disposal once again. Lock "fumbled" on the first offensive drive after it seemed like he was clearly trying to execute a basketball chest pass near a receiver's feet to avoid a sack. The refs saw it differently, and it was still a poor decision on his part. Jaxon Smith-Njigba had a TD called back on a questionable offensive PI call and had a drop on a later third down. Everything just looked disjointed. Then, on a third and long, Lock rolled out, avoided a sack, stopped just short of the line of scrimmage and threw a long TD pass to Cooper Kupp. There wasn't much after that until the third quarter where the Seahawks went wild mostly on the back of JSN. Lock found him in another scramble drill for a 71-yard TD, and the Seahawks also scored on Jadarian Price's first NFL TD showing his burst to the outside. The offense went cold again in the fourth quarter when they had the chance to salt the game away, but Brian Fleury had maybe his best call of the game with the naked bootleg to essentially end the game.

Seattle overcame a lot. Lock turned the ball over on the first drive. Abe Lucas got hurt early on leading to Bobby Hart playing RT after Josh Jones was already playing LT for the injured Charles Cross. That's in addition to Quenton Nelson, Sam Darnold, Leo Williams also on the sidelines. The rest of the games where Seattle played like crap this season, they lost. To find a way to come away with a win when giving the other team extra chances and facing a litany of injuries – on the road no less – shows grit.

The Turf Monster was busy. How many times did a Seahawks player eat dirt today after slipping on that terrible field? Charbonnet and Price both went down early multiple times. JSN actually fell down before he got loose for the 71-yard TD. Those are the worst field conditions I can remember seeing in the last number of years. I get it that the players want natural grass, but if that's going to be the result, count me out.

Spoon went blitz-crazy. Devon Witherspoon is a demon blitzing from his CB position. We saw him give Drake Maye fits in the Super Bowl, but he hasn't been utilized that way as much as I anticipated this season. Until today. Spoon blitzed three times, and came away with 2.0 sacks and a QB hit on the third one. Each time, he hammered Mendoza and I can't believe that he didn't cough the ball up. Spoon is such a weapon and brings the juice for the whole defense.

Stacking sacks. Spoon had 2.0 sacks, and the Seahawks defensive line added 4 more, one each from Derick Hall, DeMarcus Lawrence, Dante Fowler Jr, and Byron Murphy. They were a key to the second half surge against Mendoza and will look to keep the momentum going after the bye week, hopefully with Leo Williams added back into the mix.

JSN. That's it, I'm honestly running out of adjectives for his tremendous play. What can you say when a guy puts up 144 receiving yards in one quarter?? He finished with 8 catches for 178 yards and a TD. The rest of the team managed 6 catches for 69 yards. Can Seattle find someone else after the bye week to step up and take some pressure off of JSN?

The running game is coming around. I shouldn't have made it this far without mentioning the run game, but here we are. Am I crazy, or does Charbonnet actually look better now than he did before his injury? He runs ANGRY and is displaying great vision. Charbs finished with 20 carries for 94 yards and sent a bunch of dudes to the turf. Price only had 36 yards on 9 carries, yet got loose to the outside for his first TD. I'm still waiting on Price's breakout game which I do think is coming. Still, with Charbs playing as well as he is, maybe it isn't needed.

Tory Horton made one of the coolest plays ever. Seriously, Horton skying to keep the ball in bounds on the kickoff, which was then returned by Rashid Shaheed to get the ball to the two-minute warning was awesome. It might not seem like a huge deal, but the Raiders weren't dead at that point and still had 2 timeouts. With the two-minute warning, they could've stopped the clock three times and who knows what would've happened. Horton's heady play put more pressure on the Raiders, and the Seahawks ended up icing the game away. Great stuff.

With the way the Seahawks season has gone, getting to the bye week at 6-4 with a chance to heal up is just what they needed. We can all sit back and enjoy a stress-free few weeks until Seattle suits up again. Get healthy, continue to run the ball with authority, and play great defense. #2637. AC Milan identify Stiller as Modric's heir with Krösche tipped for key role

Italian source Tuttosport reports that AC Milan have identified Angelo Stiller as a possible successor to veteran Luka Modric.

When the 41-year-old hangs up his boots, there will be a creative vacuum in the Italians' midfield that Stiller could fill.

Stiller's release clause is also a key focus. The German international can leave VfB Stuttgart for a fixed transfer fee of €40million.

However, even though Stiller's contract only runs until 2028, Sky Germany recently reported that an extension seems unlikely.

It's possible that Stiller would even be available for less than the aforementioned clause this summer given his contract situation.

In Milan, Markus Krösche is also considered to be capable of playing a key role in the attempt to sign Stiller from the Swabian outfit.

The former sporting director of Eintracht Frankfurt will take over as Head of Football at the traditional Italian club on 1 January 2027.

His excellent connections in Germany and knowledge of the Bundesliga clubs could prove beneficial in a potential Stiller transfer.

#2631. MLB rumors: Tarik Skubal's market already hot, contenders eyeing Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a bit more than a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Friday's hot stove happenings.

The market for two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, far and away the offseason's best free agent, is already hot, according to the New York Post. Skubal is expected to sign in November, before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, though a deal is not imminent. Talks are underway, however, and his market is moving.

Skubal is expected to sign a record contract at least in total value, and possibly in average annual value. Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract ever given out. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander's matching $43.3 million salaries with the Mets years ago set the record for the average annual value for a pitcher.

The Dodgers, Mets, Padres, Phillies, and Yankees are among the teams linked to Japanese slugger Teruaki Sato, reports the New York Post. Unless MLB and the MLBPA unexpectedly avoid a lockout, Sato must sign before the collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1. Otherwise, he will return to the Hanshin Tigers for 2027.

We ranked Sato as the fourth-best free agent available this offseason, and the best available position player. He has significant power but also swing-and-miss and defensive concerns at third base, similar to Munetaka Murakami a year ago. Murakami slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games as a rookie this season, providing proof of concept for Sato.

The Nationals have signed center fielder Jacob Young to a four-year extension, reports FanSided. The deal is worth $23 million and includes an $8 million club option for a fifth year. The extension buys out Young's three arbitration years and one free agent year, with a club option for a second free agent year. He's now under Washington's control through 2031.

Young, 27, has always been a superlative defender. He unlocked a new level on offense this season, particularly in the second half, when he hit .301 with a .385 on-base percentage. Young had been speculated as a trade candidate since last offseason, but the new extension locks him in as part of Washington's long-term core.

#2628. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2621. Raiders winners and losers: A fast start couldn't stop Seattle's surge

The Raiders didn't commit a single penalty or turn the ball over against the Seattle Seahawks Sunday, and they still lost by eight. Clean football only carries a team so far when its offense vanishes for an entire half.

Seattle's 21-13 win at Allegiant Stadium turned on a third quarter in which the Seahawks scored twice in a span of 2:10. The Raiders (4-6) never reached the end zone again, and a 10-7 halftime lead slipped away for good.

Nevertheless, a few Raiders gave Klint Kubiak something to build on, while others let Seattle take control of the afternoon.

The defense struck on Seattle's second offensive snap. Taron Johnson and Foley Fatukasi converged on Drew Lock for a strip sack, and Quay Walker recovered at the Seattle 46 to hand the offense a short field.

Nakobe Dean pounced on another Lock fumble in the fourth quarter, and Jason Myers missed a 44-yard field goal. Better still, holding Seattle to 21 points snapped a streak of six straight games allowing 30 or more.

For two quarters, the rookie looked comfortable in the pocket and outside of it. Mendoza completed 11 of 13 passes for 90 yards and capped his first drive with a 10-yard scramble for his first NFL touchdown.

He added 21 rushing yards on five carries before halftime, giving Seattle's defense one more thing to chase. The Raiders scored 10 points on his first two possessions against a defense that came in allowing 18 points per game.

No Raider logged more work than the punter. Cole punted seven times for a 56.4-yard average, and his 50.0 net average with three kicks inside the 20 pinned Seattle deep all afternoon.

With the offense handing him the ball so often, Cole made sure field position never became a second problem.

A week after Kirk Cousins dropped back 32 times in Santa Clara without being sacked, the line couldn't keep Seattle off the rookie. Mendoza went down six times and absorbed 12 hits, with cornerback Devon Witherspoon sacking him twice.

Four of those sacks came after halftime, so every third-and-long turned into a fight for survival.

The wheels came off once an ankle injury ruled Brock Bowers out for the second half. After Matt Gay's second-quarter field goal, the Raiders punted on seven straight possessions and gained 24 yards in that stretch.

They also went 0-for-7 on third down after halftime, and Kubiak didn't sugarcoat it.

He later said the Raiders' second-half third-down performance was unacceptable.

Raiders Wire made Smith-Njigba the pre-game Gimme Him pick for this matchup, and he used the second half to show the Raiders why. After one catch for 11 yards before the break, he caught seven passes for 160 yards, including a 71-yard touchdown that made it 21-10.

His big day helped Lock finish 14 of 17 for 240 yards and a career-best 158.0 passer rating, a stunning line for a backup quarterback.

#2620. MLB free agency: Six international players to know for the 2026-27 offseason

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Major League Baseball's free agency period opened earlier this week and teams are now clear to pursue any roster upgrades they deem necessary. That includes players coming over from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball league, South Korea's Korea Baseball Organization, and Taiwan's Chinese Professional Baseball League. Those are high-level leagues that have sent many impact players MLB's way over the years.

Look no farther than the Dodgers to see how important international talent can be to a club. The Dodgers employed four different former NPB and KBO players this past season, including two-way star Shohei Ohtani, ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, and starter Roki Sasaki. Ohtani was signed as an MLB free agent, but the others went to the Dodgers through the posting system.

Per the posting agreement with MLB, posted NPB and CPBL players get a 45-day window to negotiate and sign with an MLB team. KBO players get a 30-day window. Players who do not sign during that posting window return to their previous team in NPB, CPBL, or KBO. The MLB team that signs a posted player pays a fee to the player's former NPB, CPBL, or KBO team.

$5M plus 17.5% of contract value over $25M

$9.375M plus 15% of contract value over $50M

For example, the White Sox paid Munetaka Murakami's former team, the Yakult Swallows, a $6.575 million posting fee on his $34 million contract last offseason. That's $5 million on the first $25 million plus 17.5% of the remaining $9 million, which is $1.575 million. The $5 million plus $1.575 million equals the $6.575 million posting fee paid to the Swallows.

Unlike last lockout, MLB will not be pausing the signing window during the expected lockout, according to The Athletic. In other words, if owners lock players out on Dec. 1 as expected, that date will essentially serve as the same deadline for already posted NPB players unless the lockout ends before their 45-day window expires.

There are no superstar-caliber players like Ohtani or Yamamoto available in this winter's international free agent crop. There are, however, several interesting players who can improve an MLB roster in 2027. Here are the six best NPB, CPBL, and KBO players to know this offseason.

Japan's Triple Crown winner hit .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs in 2026. He has a similar skill set to Murakami but is not exactly Murakami 2.0. He doesn't have quite as much power (but has plenty of it) and won't walk nearly as often, but he does swing and miss a bunch and is unlikely to remain at the hot corner long-term. Sato is a very aggressive hitter who ran a 66% contact rate this past season. That is below the 77% MLB average. The consensus seems to be that he will land at first base or in a corner outfield spot if not next year, then soon. Murakami successfully overcame his contact issues to slug 35 homers in only 127 games in 2026 around a hamstring injury. At minimum, that will have MLB teams reconsidering how they evaluate the Japan-to-MLB transition. Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll. The Hanshin Tigers officially posted Sato on Nov. 1.

Listed at 5-foot-8, Taira gets outlier extension down the mound (close to seven feet despite his height), which creates a low release window. Hitters rarely see the ball come from where Taira releases it. He's not a gimmick pitcher either. Taira sits mid-90s with his four-seam fastball and backs it up with a cutter, sinker, sweeper, slider, changeup, and splitter. The sweeper and slider are distinct pitches, as are the changeup and splitter. The Seibu Lions used Taira as a reliever in 2024 and 2025, then started him in 2026, and he handled the assignment well. The breaking balls are just OK, and the fact of the matter is that pitchers this height don't often hold up under a starter's workload. I would assume the team that signs Taira will give him a chance to start. In the long run, though, he might be a reliever, perhaps even a multi-inning setup man. Taira was officially posted on Nov. 1.

A down 2026 season took some of the shine off Itoh, who won the 2025 Eiji Sawamura Award (Japan's Cy Young equivalent) after throwing 196 ⅔ innings with a 2.52 ERA. To be sure, Itoh pitched well in 2026 (3.18 ERA in 172 ⅔ innings), but he was not as consistently dominant as in the past. The 5-foot-9 right-hander is a seven-pitch pitcher with a low-90s fastball and the usual array of secondary pitches (sinker, cutter, curveball, slider, sweeper, splitter), none of which stands out as a plus offering. Itoh has thrown at least 150 innings in each of the last six seasons. He's seen as a crafty back-end starter in MLB, or perhaps even a reliever (Itoh sat 96 mph out of the bullpen in the World Baseball Classic). The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Itoh on Nov. 1.

Roh has an unusual agreement with the Hanwha Eagles. He signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and roughly $23 million), and as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him for MLB teams this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the Eagles to finish his career when his big-league stint is over. This past season, Roh, 26 in November, authored a .283/.360/.505 batting line with 29 home runs. He has real right-handed power and a good approach at the plate. There are concerns about his propensity to swing and miss as well as his arm at the hot corner. The Eagles formally posted Roh on Nov. 1.

The Seibu Lions posted Takahashi last offseason, but he was unable to find a contract to his liking, so he returned to Japan for another season and threw 148 innings with a 2.64 ERA. Takahashi, 30 in February, is an international free agent now, meaning he does not have to be posted and can instead negotiate at his own pace. More of a ground ball pitcher than a bat-misser, Takahashi sits in the 91-95 mph range with his fastball and has two good secondary pitches in his slider and splitter. He also throws a cutter and curveball. Takahashi is considered a potential innings guy for the back of an MLB rotation.

Tseng pitched for Chinese Taipei in the World Baseball Classic in 2023 and 2026 and he has been one of the CPBL's top relievers the last few years. In 2026, he saved 25 games with a 1.80 ERA and 65 strikeouts in 52 ⅓ innings. Tseng's fastball typically sits in the mid-90s and has run as high as 100 mph in the past, though it has been a few years. His go-to secondary pitch is a breaking ball that needs improvement for Tseng to carve out an MLB career as more than a middle reliever.

#2617. MLB rumors: Why the Dodgers could be Tarik Skubal or bust; Red Sox looking for pitching depth

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest thing hanging over baseball this offseason is obviously the expiration of the CBA and what everyone assumes will be a lockout. Until then, we'll find out the major award winners this coming week, starting with Rookies of the Year on Monday. And, of course, there's the player movement yet to come.

For the latter, let's round up Sunday's rumors right here.

As we saw plenty in 2026, the Dodgers have a very talented rotation with a few injury-prone parts (Tyler Glasnow, Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher, etc.). As such, this bit of speculative reporting from The Athletic makes a ton of sense:

The Dodgers will need someone who can cover innings in 2027. It's just a matter of how much they can lean on Justin Wrobleski, trust how Emmet Sheehan finished the season (I'd say probably a good amount), how healthy Gavin Stone is (unknown), how ready Jackson Ferris is (he seems close) and if they have enough depth options behind them.

All that to say, the Dodgers will be in on Skubal. If he goes elsewhere, I don't think it's as simple as the Dodgers going after the next highest-ranked starter on the market, such as a Freddy Peralta or a Michael King. I could see them taking a flier on some depth options to soak up innings in anticipation of a quick ramp-up post-lockout, sort of like they did when they signed Tyler Anderson in the run-up to the 2022 season.

Yes, the Dodgers are in on the Tarik Skubal bidding. We all know that. But if they lose out on retaining the two-time Cy Young winner, they may not just continue moving down the list for available starters. Then again, it's hard to ever know exactly what Andrew Friedman is going to spend money on.

As things stand, the Dodgers' rotation has Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Snell, Glasnow, Roki Sasaki and Sheehan, at least until Ohtani is ready to rejoin the fray.

Coming off two straight Wild Card Series losses and sub-90-win seasons, the Red Sox would surely like to take things up a notch for the 2027 season. One way might be to build out the depth of the pitching staff. They'll be "in the market for a back-end starter" and a right-handed reliever "with swing-and-miss capability," according to MassLive.

For the rotation: Sonny Gray hits free agency, but Garrett Crochet will return from a nearly full-season injury. Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez fill the 2-3 spots, with Jake Bennett solid as the No. 4. That leaves Brayan Bello, Kutter Crawford and Tanner Houck as options for the fifth spot in addition to depth. It doesn't seem dire, but we've seen plenty of times what kind of havoc injuries can wreak.

In the bullpen, lefty Aroldis Chapman returns at closer with Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller as setup men. Houck missing out on a rotation spot could mean he helps late as well.

Fabio Caressa ha risposto alle critiche per aver urlato meno del previsto durante il gol di Davide Frattesi contro la Francia, quello del momentaneo 2-1. #2614. Penn State holds dominant 33-2 series lead over Rutgers

Penn State has given itself a strong chance of winning out to end this season. After three straight wins against Big Ten teams, the Nittany Lions get to play an opponent who they have dominated throughout their history.

The Rutgers Scarlet Knights are coming to town this week, and they'll be looking for their first win against the blue and white in nearly 40 years. They won the first ever matchup between these two teams in 1918, but then they went another 60 years before they beat the Nittany Lions again.

Penn State holds a 33-2 all-time record in the series, and it is 33-1 since the first matchup with Rutgers when football was still in its infancy. However, both of its losses have come at home, so the team needs to make sure it doesn't sleepwalk through this game.

There were some offensive fireworks last year when these clubs faced off. The Nittany Lions won 40-36 thanks to impressive showings from running backs Kaytron Allen and Nicholas Singleton.

Allen had 22 carries for 226 yards and a touchdown, while Singleton carried the ball nine times for 86 yards and two touchdowns.

Scarlet Knights receiver KJ Duff also had a big day, catching five passes for 127 yards and a touchdown. However, he was recently ruled out for the season, so Penn State won't see him this time around.

The blue and white have had a stranglehold on this series for more than 75 years now, so let's see if they maintain that edge.

#2613. MLB rumors: Why the Cubs may already be out on Tarik Skubal, plus latest on Phillies, Cardinals, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The uncertain 2026-27 Major League Baseball offseason is fully underway. The ongoing CBA negotiations and the near certainty of an owner-implemented lockout on Dec. 2 loom over all, and it may indeed mean a flurry of trades and free agent signings leading up to that date. That was certainly the case leading up to the last lockout of 2021-22.

Thanks to that prospect of a hastened pace, offseason rumors are already flowing. Speaking of which, we'll be here each day to round up what's out there. You can find Monday's supply just below.

The expectation remains that we'll see some level of activity on the trade and free agency fronts before the lockout begins in early December. As noted above, that was indeed the case leading up to the last lockout, and this time around, the prospect of drastic changes in the next CBA may have big-spending teams looking to fortify their rosters before those changes are implemented. Speaking of which, MLB Network reports that we could see some notable transactions go down at the upcoming General Managers Meetings, which take place from Nov. 10-12 in Las Vegas.

During a standard offseason, not much beyond behind-the-scenes groundwork goes down during the GM Meetings, and the real moves start happening at the December Winter Meetings. However, unless the lockout is resolved quickly – highly unlikely – then there probably won't be a Winter Meetings this offseason. That means the GM Meetings could be more active than usual.

Free agent ace and, until later this week, reigning back-to-back  American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal is the prize of the offseason. The 29-year-old lefty is a fit for any of MLB's 30 teams, but heretofore the most serious bidders have been expected to be the Los Angeles Dodgers (who acquired Skubal from the Detroit Tigers leading up to last season's trade deadline), the New York Mets, and the Chicago Cubs. Now, though, perhaps you can reduce that number of serious bidders to two. While Chicago very much needs rotation help for 2027 and beyond, the Athletic reports that the Cubs "are expected to stay on the sidelines" when the Skubal bidding gets serious. That, no doubt, will come as a disappointment to Cubs fans who are still waiting for the Ricketts to invest in the payroll at levels befitting a big-market contender.

The Cardinals traded away veteran lefty reliever JoJo Romero, along with starter and fellow free agent Dustin May, to the Milwaukee Brewers leading up to the trade deadline. Now, St. Louis may be interested in bringing Romero back on a free agent contract, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reports.

Romero, 30, is coming off a 2026 season in which he pitched to a 3.36 ERA with a 3.00 K/BB ratio in 55 appearances. In the postseason with Milwaukee, Romero had a 1.13 ERA with 11 strikeouts and one walk in eight innings. He previously spent parts of five seasons with the Cardinals.

Do the Philadelphia Phillies need a new shortstop? That's one of the principal questions of their offseason. Although incumbent Trea Turner is signed through 2033, his defense at the crucial position of shortstop has degraded into "unplayable" territory, and that has the Phils considering fallback options should Turner need to be moved off the position. One option is free agent 31-year-old Ha-Seong Kim, NBC Sports Philadelphia reports. Kim, 32, spent last season on a one-year deal with the division-rival Atlanta Braves. He's been a primary shortstop for five of his six MLB seasons, and while he's certainly not among the very best at the position, he does profile as a major defensive upgrade over Turner. As for the bat, Kim for his career has an OPS+ of 93, and he's capable of stealing a base on occasion. He was, however, an offensive sinkhole for 51 games in 2026. Turner, meantime, may be looking at a switch to the outfield starting next season as the Phillies attempt to keep their contending window open.

#2611. Predicting 2027 MLB Rookie of the Year candidates: Josue De Paula, Kade Anderson, Jesús Made and more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle and Reds slugger Sal Stewart were named the 2026 Rookies of the Year on Monday night. McGonigle was the wire-to-wire leader for the award despite a stacked American League rookie class. In the National League, Stewart edged out Mets outfielder Carson Benge and Cardinals second baseman JJ Wetherholt, both of whom had excellent rookie campaigns.

No award gets you excited about the future the way Rookie of the Year does. It's a young player being recognized for his greatness, and great young players are what sports hopes are built on. With that in mind, here's a look ahead at the 2027 rookie class and, more importantly, who could be in the running for the 2027 Rookie of the Year awards.

Anderson made his debut in late August and gave the Mariners seven solid starts, though he remains rookie-eligible because he did not exceed the rookie limits of 50 innings or 45 days of service time. Anderson, the No. 3 pick in the 2025 Draft, is arguably the best pitching prospect in the game and is likely to have a rotation spot on Opening Day, which figures to boost his Rookie of the Year case. Add in a pitcher-friendly home ballpark, and Anderson is the super early favorite for the award. He had 167 strikeouts against only 22 walks in 129 innings between MLB and the minors in 2026.

One of the best prospects in the minors, Arias nearly made his MLB debut in September, but the Red Sox opted against it. He authored a .323/.400/.557 line with 25 home runs between Double-A and Triple-A in 2026, including a .331/.388/.506 line in 42 games at Triple-A as a 20-year-old. Trevor Story is entering the final year of his contract and has been healthy and productive at the same time once in the last four years. Arias likely gives Boston a better chance to win right now and I would not be surprised to see them turn the shortstop reins over to the youngster early next season. Early as in April.

Like Anderson, Jenkins made his MLB debut in late August, yet his rookie eligibility remains intact going into 2027. He had a rough go of it in the majors, slashing .226/.293/.393 in 26 games with the Twins, though his contact rates and plate discipline were impressive. Jenkins will turn only 22 in February and he is not the first top prospect to have a rough 26 games to begin his big-league career, nor will he be the last. There might be more growing pains to come next season, but Minnesota figures to give Jenkins a long runway to work through them. His 2027 could look like Benge's 2026, meaning sluggish early and sensational late.

It was only 11 games (plus four pinch-hitting appearances in the postseason), but gosh, De Paula was so impressive during his big-league debut. He's a precocious hitter with tremendous strike zone knowledge (13 walks and five strikeouts), and also some serious hard-hit ability. The biggest obstacle standing between De Paula and next year's Rookie of the Year award is playing time. Shohei Ohtani is locked in at DH and Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker aren't going anywhere. The Dodgers will have to either trade or bench Teoscar Hernández to get De Paula into the lineup. It would be worth it. The Yordan Alvarez comps De Paula got in the minors don't seem so insane now.

The Brewers are the World Series champions and they also have arguably the best farm system in the game with the consensus No. 1 prospect in Made. Still only 19, Made performed admirably in a full season at Double-A this year, and he's currently playing very well against grown men in the Dominican Winter League. He figures to open next season in Triple-A, with a May or June promotion to Milwaukee in the cards. That could put Made at a disadvantage in the Rookie of the Year race. Either way, it's only a matter of time until the defending champions add the game's best prospect to their lineup, presumably at third base.

At 20 years and 121 days, Salas became the youngest catcher to ever appear in a postseason game in Game 2 of this year's Wild Card Series. He started three of San Diego's six postseason games after making his MLB debut in September, and it seems likely Salas will take over as their starting backstop next season. I think he's a longshot Rookie of the Year candidate simply because it's really hard to be a rookie catcher, and next year Salas will be the youngest regular catcher since Hall of Famer Ivan Rodriguez in 1991. Still, Salas is a special defender with promising offensive chops.

Several prominent Japanese veterans will make their way to MLB via the posting system this offseason. We don't know where they will sign yet, but the rules say these players will be Rookie of the Year-eligible regardless of their age or years of experience in Japan, so we're going to include them here.

We ranked Sato as the best position player free agent on the market this offseason. Japan's reigning Triple Crown winner has tremendous left-handed power. We're talking legitimate 30-homer upside. Sato does swing and miss a bunch, though, and he's an aggressive hitter who's unlikely to walk as much as Munetaka Murakami, which could hold him back at the plate. Add in questionable defense at the hot corner and it's unclear exactly how much impact Sato will have in the big leagues. Bottom line though, guys with 30-homer power will always be in the Rookie of the Year conversation.

Taira, our No. 19 free agent, is destined to be a fan favorite given his fire hydrant build (5-foot-8 and 220 lbs.) and bat-missing fastball. He gets close to seven feet of extension down the mound despite his height, creating a unique release window and an "upshoot" effect on his fastball. Taira started for the Seibu Lions in 2026 after spending 2024 and 2025 in the bullpen. I assume the team that signs him will give him a chance to start next year. If he winds up in relief, Taira has the stuff and gumption to get high-leverage outs in the late innings.

But after a miserable 2026 season, the asking price for Duran has likely dropped significantly, which could make a trade more likely.

Jarren Duran first came up in 2021, and was a regular by 2023. In 2024 he broke through as an All-Star, hitting .285/.342/.492 with 21 home runs and 34 steals. He led the league in doubles (48) and triples (14) and put up a whopping 9.0 rWAR, third-most in the American League. His numbers regressed in 2025 to .256/.332/.442, but he still hit 16 home runs and stole 24 bases, and was a 4.9 rWAR player. His power, speed, and defense still made him a very attractive player that would require a large return.

But the bottom fell out for Duran in 2026. He got off to a dreadful start and was under the Mendoza Line as late as August. He hit just .207/.266/.361, and while he finished the season with 20 home runs and 21 steals, but it is one of the worst 20/20 seasons in MLB history. He is still one of the fastest runners in baseball, and he performed well defensively according to Outs Above Average and Defensive Runs Saved.

What happened to Duran's bat? He has always been a weak hitter against lefties, but this year he failed to hit righties as well. He had a rise in strikeout rate to 27.1 percent while his walk rate dropped to 6.7 percent. If you look at his Baseball Savant page, you can see his whiff rate rose against breaking balls and off-speed pitches.

But perhaps the biggest difference is how he hit fastballs. In 2025, he was a .275 hitter against heaters, with a .274 xBA. This year, he was a .226 hitter against heaters, with a .273 xBA. In other words, Duran may not have been hitting fastballs any worse, he was just getting some bad luck. His overall BABIP this year was just .252, down from .326 in 2025. On the other hand, his exit velocity, hard-hit rate, and barrel rate all fell, ominous signs for a hitter.

Duran has spoken openly about his struggles with mental health, including a suicide attempt. In the Netflix documentary The Clubhouse, Duran is shown being extremely hard on himself, something teammates have tried to help him manage. He plays with a very intense style, but that intensity has occasionally spilled over into confrontations with fans, including an incident at Kauffman Stadium early in his career.

Duran is 30 years old and has two more years of club control. He is projected to earn around $11 million through arbitration, although he is also a non-tender candidate. The Red Sox have a very crowded outfield with Roman Anthony, Cedanne Rafaela, and Wilyer Abreu likely to start, and designated hitter was filled by the signing of Jake Bauers last week. That should make them pretty motivated sellers for Duran.

Duran would certainly address a major need for the Royals. He is a left-handed hitter with power and speed who could immediately slot into the leadoff spot. His ability to play center field would also give the Royals some additional flexibility, even if they primarily envision him in left field. If he can recapture anything close to his 2024 form, he would be a significant upgrade to a position that has been a black hole offensively for Kansas City.

But there is considerable risk. Duran is coming off a season in which he was one of the least productive regular hitters in baseball. His declining contact rates and increased struggles against breaking pitches are concerning, and the Royals would have to determine whether those problems are correctable or signs of a more permanent decline. They would also be acquiring a player whose emotional intensity has occasionally become a distraction.

Because he is such a gamble, it likely won't take much to acquire him at this point. The Royals could look for a swap of bad contracts and send Seth Lugo to Boston. But that seems unlikely with the Royals also valuing starting pitching depth and Boston unlikely to want to take on the contract. Instead, the Royals may part ways with a token prospect or two and simply take on the risk of Duran. If he returns to form, the upside could be huge. And if he is terrible, the Royals can simply non-tender him in a year.

The Royals have spent three years searching for an answer in left field. While Duran would be a gamble, buying low on a player with his talent could be a worthwhile risk.

#2609. Connor Hellebuyck trade: Jets send star goalie to the Devils in exchange for four players, two draft picks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Connor Hellebuyck is a now a Devil. The star goalie for the Winnipeg Jets is on the move after being traded to New Jersey on Friday in exchange for four players and two future draft picks. the teams announced the move with the Jets receiving Dawson Mercer, Nick Bjugstad, Nico Daws and Alexander Command, plus a 2027 seventh-round pick and a 2029 second-round pick.

Hellebuyck expressed his desire to be traded in the offseason when he formally requested a move in August. He said at the time that he had made the request months earlier and tried to keep the situation private.

Hellebuyck has spent his entire career with Winnipeg after being drafted by the Jets in 2012 at No. 130 overall. He's recognized as one of the best goalies in the league as a three-time Vezina Trophy winner. He also helped carry the United States to its first gold medal since 1980 at the 2026 Olympics in February with some incredible saves against Canada in the final game.

After trading Jacob Markstom in the offseason, the Devils had a clear need in goal, and this splashy move certainly fills that need. With a talented young core already in place, New Jersey's Stanley Cup window is wide open.

RAISE HELLE!Connor Hellebuyck is a New Jersey Devil: https://t.co/HCehRGOQI5 pic.twitter.com/dZGNQR16m1

For the Jets, it must be a hard pill to swallow when a franchise icon decides to walk out they door, but this trade package should help them as the enter a new era and revamp the roster. Winnipeg got a former first-rounder in Mercer to try and add to a rebuild as well as a veteran presence in Bjugstad. They also acquired a younger goalie in Daws who could fill the role of Hellebuyck at just 25 years old.

Goaltending has been an issue in New Jersey for a while now -- even after the team acquired Markstrom from the Calgary Flames in 2024. Markstom never really panned out, and his 13.6 goals allowed above average, per Natural Stat Trick, were a big reason why the Devils missed the postseason last year.

In the early portion of this season, it was clear that New Jersey needed to make a move to upgrade in the crease. Daws and veteran Jake Allen simply aren't a tandem suitable for a Stanley Cup contender, and the numbers backed that up. New Jersey ranks 24th in team save percentage at .877, and the duo of Daws and Allen combined to surrender 2.99 goals above average.

Once Hellebuyck gets up to game speed, that shouldn't be a problem anymore.

In the three-season stretch from 2023-26, Hellebuyck led the NHL with 73.42 goals saved above average, which is 20 goals higher than the next closest netminder. Over that span, Hellebuyck also posted a standard save percentage of .914 and an astronomical high-danger save-percentage of .832.

Hellebuyck carried less talented teams to the playoffs multiple times in his career. Now on a team loaded with weaponry in their prime -- Jack Hughes, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier to name a few -- Hellebuyck could be the final piece to the championship puzzle.

In terms of the acquisition cost, it was probably an easy deal for Devils general manager Sunny Mehta to make. The 2029 second-round pick is useless for a team that should be all-in now, Bjugstad is simply a depth piece and Daws now has no path to a starting role with Hellebuyck in town.

The most interesting trade chips are Mercer and Command. Mercer flashed major upside with 56 points in his second NHL season, 2022-23, but he hasn't really come close to hitting those heights again. Still, even if he has plateaued, Mercer remains a strong middle-six forward rising into his prime.

Although Command had his detractors -- and may have been over-drafted at No. 12 overall -- he was a consensus first-round pick last summer. That gives Winnipeg a potential franchise forward it can build around long-term, but New Jersey already has one of the deepest forward groups in the league, especially with the emergence of Arseny Gritsyuk and the acquisition of Luke Evangelista.

If we're looking for a 3-D chess angle of this deal, it only makes the Devils more appealing for a certain Minnesota Wild defenseman whose brothers just happen to play in New Jersey already. Grade -- A+

Let's get the obvious out of the way first: The Jets were never going to get fair value for Hellebuyck because, at his best, he's the No. 1 goaltender in the world with no equal. That type of excellence can't be replaced.

That said, Winnipeg did fairly well given the circumstances. Hellebuyck made a public trade request, and he wasn't even with the team after sitting out for the entirety of training camp. The entire league knew the Jets had to trade him.

Hellebuyck's talent created a decent market anyway, but most of the suitors were bona fide Stanley Cup contenders with little in the way of valuable draft capital, and they weren't going to knee cap the roster by sending a key player back in return.

With all that taken into consideration, Kevin Cheveldayoff got a solid return. Although Mercer's ceiling may be lower than initially thought, he's a 24-year-old forward who banks roughly 20 goals and 20 assists every season. The kicker with Mercer will be Winnipeg's ability to re-sign him before he hits restricted free agency next summer.

The addition of Command means Winnipeg now has two forwards selected in the top 12 of the 2026 NHL Draft after taking center Viggo Bjorck themselves. If both of those players deliver on their first-round pedigrees, they could be a terrific one-two punch for the team long-term.

Daws was a third-round pick in 2020, and despite playing just 13 NHL games since the start of the 2024-25 season, he should give Winnipeg a solid back up option behind Stuart Skinner. It certainly helps that Skinner is off to a great start with his new team -- and if Daws develops into a true No. 1 -- it'll be gravy.

If there's any reason to critique this deal from the Jets' side of things, it's that they didn't get premium draft capital or a surefire up-and-coming prospect. Maybe Command develops into a star, but there's no guarantee he becomes a top-six stud in the NHL.

The Jets got a lot of good stuff, but they didn't really get anything great, at least not based on what we know in the moment. Because of that, I have to ding Winnipeg a little bit. Grade: B

#2602. 2026 MLB Rookie of the Year: Tigers' Kevin McGonigle, Reds' Sal Stewart win BBWAA awards

Kevin McGonigle of the Tigers and Sal Stewart of the Reds were named the 2026 Rookies of the Year in their respective leagues on Monday night as part of the BBWAA's awards week. McGonigle earned 28 of 30 first-place votes, beating out the Guardians' Parker Messick and the Red Sox's Payton Tolle. Stewart, meanwhile, beat the Mets' Carson Benge and the Cardinals' JJ Wetherholt.

Because McGonigle and Stewart were both with the major-league team for long enough to earn a full year of service time, the Tigers and Reds will each receive a Prospect Promotion Incentive pick in the 2027 MLB Draft.

The annual awards, which also include Manager of the Year, Reliever of the Year, Cy Young and MVP, are voted on by 30 members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (that's two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

Stewart won the battle of Old School stats vs. New School stats here. Though he only posted 2.0 WAR, he had 32 home runs and 111 RBI, putting him in rarefied air for a rookie. He's one of just 15 rookies ever with at least 30 homers and 100 RBI. The only names from that list to not win the award either faced another player from the list or played before Rookie of the Year was awarded. Everyone else has taken home the hardware, just as Stewart did Monday evening.

Overall, Stewart appeared in all 162 games, hitting .263/.330/.457 (117 OPS+) with 25 doubles, 32 homers, 112 RBI, 87 runs and 15 steals.

Stewart earned 20 of the 30 available first-place votes.

Carson Benge of the Mets finished second and JJ Wetherholt of the Cardinals finished in third place. Benge, the 2024 first-rounder, made the team out of spring training and hit .282/.346/.430 with 20 home runs, 22 steals and 4.3 WAR. Defensive metrics love Wetherholt and helped push him to 4.5 WAR in 139 games. He hit .242/.339/.365 with 17 homers, 14 steals and 89 runs.

Stewart joins the following Reds as Rookie of the Year winners:

The honor for McGonigle completes a stellar year for the former first-round draft pick. He broke camp with the Tigers and was productive from the get-go. He ended up hitting .278/.376/.430 (126 OPS+) with 28 doubles, five triples, 18 home runs, 72 RBI, 97 runs, 12 steals and 7.1 WAR, the latter good enough for the AL lead among position players. He played great defense, ran the bases well and was an All-Star. He nearly walked (95) as much as he struck out (100), too. Not much more could've been asked of the Pennsylvania native who played most of the season at age 21, and he's a well-deserving Rookie of the Year.

A few weeks after he debuted, he and the team agreed to an eight-year, $150 million extension.

McGonigle won in a blowout, getting 28 of the 30 available first-place votes, scoring 204 of a possible 210 points.

He joins the following players who have won the award with the Tigers:

Parker Messick of the Guardians finishes second after going 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 193 strikeouts in 186 ⅓ innings; he is also a top-three finalist for the Cy Young award. Red Sox starter Payton Tolle finishes third after going 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA (135 ERA+), 1.10 WHIP and 171 strikeouts in 148 ⅔ innings.

#2601. ESPN diagnoses biggest problem for the Falcons

The Atlanta Falcons have no shortage of problems going into their bye week. Their once-feisty defense has fallen into the basement in coverage, against the run and pressuring the quarterback.

That's put a lot of strain on their offense, and the results have not been pretty. On Sunday, the Falcons lost 35-13 to a Kansas City Chiefs team missing a few key starters, including Kenneth Walker.

Fundamentally, Atlanta's biggest problem right now is that the offense is not running through the best running back on the planet. ESPN detailed the problem in their Week 10 takeaways.

"...The Falcons have scored a combined 30 points the past three games. Atlanta was at its best when it was imposing its will with the running game, led by star Bijan Robinson. The Falcons have been unable to get Robinson going like he was during that stretch in Weeks 3-7, even though he came into Sunday leading the league in rushing. A more potent ground attack is the only way to take the pressure off quarterback Michael Penix Jr."

The solution isn't as simple as running the ball more and passing less. In order to move their offense through Bijan Robinson, the Falcons have to establish a lead early in the game. That way they can lean on Robinson rather than forcing Penix to lead a comeback.

The one exception to this rule was Atlanta's stunning win over the San Francisco 49ers - although that feels like a long time ago now and appears to have been a mirage.

This offense is only going to work if it's Robinson carrying the load. As head coach Kevin Stefanski admitted following Sunday's loss to the Kansas City Chiefs, the Falcons simply have to find a way to start games better.

This article originally appeared on Falcons Wire: ESPN diagnoses biggest problem for the Falcons

#2599. Bob Boone, All-Star catcher, 1980 World Series champion and father of Yankees manager, dies at 78

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Bob Boone, a four-time All-Star catcher and the middle member of a three-generation baseball family, has died. He was 78. His son, Bret Boone, made the announcement on Tuesday. No cause of death was given.

My dad- He was my mentor, my coach, my rock. He taught me how to be a pro and more importantly, how to be a man. He was one of the highest integrity people I’ve ever known and I’m going to miss him dearly. Baseball lost a great one yesterday. R.I.P dad, I love you❤️ pic.twitter.com/4NtYAwXIv3

"Bob Boone had an enduring impact on the field as a 19-year MLB veteran, a seven-time Gold Glove Award-winning catcher, a four-time All-Star and 1980 World Champion with the Philadelphia Phillies," the MLB Players Association said in a statement. "He embraced a leadership role in the Players Association early in his career, and earned a reputation as a strong and principled voice in the advancement of player rights in the 1970s and '80s ... As we honor Bob's legacy and mourn his passing, we extend our heartfelt condolences to his wife, Sue, sons Aaron, Bret and Matt, his extended family, and his many fans and admirers throughout the game."

The Boones were baseball's first three-generation family. Bob's father, Ray Boone, played for six teams from 1948-60, and his sons Aaron and Bret both had long careers spanning the 1990s and 2000s. Bob's other son, Matt, played in the minor leagues.

"I'm just so grateful that I had a dad that took us to work with him all the time," Aaron, now manager of the New York Yankees, said in 2023 (via MLB.com). "He came up at the end of '72, and I was born in the spring of '73. He played until my senior year in high school and literally I was at the ballpark -- my brothers and I, in unis, shagging (fly balls) and doing everything you could possibly imagine. It was a great way to grow up."

Born in San Diego, Bob Boone made his MLB debut with the Phillies in 1972 and took over as the club's starting catcher in 1973. He hit 10 home runs and finished third in the National League Rookie of the Year voting. That started a 17-year run as one of the game's best and most durable catchers. Boone started at least 130 games behind the plate eight times in his career and 110 games 14 times.

With the Phillies in 1980, Boone went 7 for 17 (.412) with four walks and zero strikeouts in Philadelphia's six-game World Series win over the Kansas City Royals.

A seven-time Gold Glove winner, including four straight during his age-38 to -41 seasons, Boone had his most productive years with the Phillies from 1976-79. He hit .282/.351/.414 those four seasons and averaged nine home runs, which was excellent output given the offensive standard at the catcher position during that era. Boone went to four All-Star Games and received MVP votes twice.

"Bob was an incredible player, teammate and family man," the Phillies said in a statement. "He embodied everything we believe exemplary athletes should represent, both on and off the field. We were proud to have him as part of the Phillies family during one of the most historic runs in team history. His impact on our organization, his teammates, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him will never be forgotten."

Boone ranks second with 2,161 games at catcher during the Modern Era (since 1900), behind only Hall of Famer Ivan Rodriguez (2,377). He is 15th among primary catchers with 1,838 hits and 21st with 2,508 total bases. Boone played parts of 19 big league seasons with the Phillies (1972-81), California Angels (1982-88), and Royals (1989-90).

The Orlando SunRays, a potential expansion franchise, hired Boone to be their manager soon after he retired as a player, though the expansion franchises were instead awarded to Denver and Miami in 1991. Boone later managed the Royals from 1995-97 and the Cincinnati Reds (2001-03). He managed his son, Aaron, those years with the Reds.

In 2005, Boone joined the Washington Nationals as their director of player development and had a hand in building the core that won the franchise's first World Series title in 2019. He remained with the Nationals until 2021. Boone spent five years on the Hall of Fame ballot from 1996 to 2000 but was not voted into Cooperstown.

#2597. Tare: Muriqi scelse la Lazio, rifiutando il PSG e uno stipendio più che doppio

L’ex direttore sportivo racconta l’aereo privato diretto a Parigi e torna sul rendimento dell’attaccante in biancoceleste.

Vedat Muriqi rifiutò il PSG per trasferirsi alla Lazio e rinunciò anche a una proposta superiore a più del doppio dello stipendio. A raccontarlo è Igli Tare, ex direttore sportivo biancoceleste, intervenuto a Sky Calcio Unplugged. Le sue parole, riprese da Chiamarsi Bomber, riguardano sia la scelta dell’attaccante kosovaro sia la sua esperienza a Roma.

CLICCA QUI E SEGUI LAZIOPRESS.IT ANCHE SU INSTAGRAM

Tare riconosce che il centravanti non riuscì a esprimere pienamente il proprio potenziale in biancoceleste. Al tempo stesso ne difende le qualità: «Parliamo di un centravanti fenomenale per il modo di interpretare il gioco e alla Lazio, per vari motivi, non ha dato quello che poteva dare».

Il giudizio dell’ex dirigente distingue dunque il valore attribuito al calciatore dal rendimento avuto alla Lazio. La sua esperienza nella Capitale non rispettò del tutto le aspettative iniziali, soprattutto sul piano realizzativo, pur senza cambiare la valutazione di Tare sulle sue capacità.

#2596. Nikita Kucherov trade request: Five potential landing spots for the reigning NHL MVP

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

One of the greatest players in Tampa Bay Lightning history may soon be wearing a different jersey. According to Sportsnet, Nikita Kucherov has told the Lightning he won't sign a contract extension and has requested a trade.

Kucherov, a two-time Stanley Cup champion and two-time Hart Trophy winner as league MVP, is one of the best players of his era. The 33-year-old just passed the legendary Steven Stamkos for the all-time franchise lead in points and has shown no signs of slowing down.

Just last season, Kucherov posted 44 goals and 86 assists en route to his second Hart Trophy win. His underlying numbers were even better with a five-on-five goal differential of plus-38 and an expected goals share of 57.0 percent. Only a select few players can drive play from the wing like Kucherov, and that makes him a unicorn of sorts.

Kucherov is in the final year of a contract that pays him $9.5 million per season, and with the salary cap rising rapidly, he's due for a gargantuan raise next summer. It sounds like Kucherov and the Lightning were too far apart on that number, so the superstar winger has shifted his focuse to a change of scenery.

It's important to note that Kucherov has limited trade protection in the form of a 10-team trade list, but that should be more than enough for the Lightning to find a suitable trade partner. With that in mind, let's take a look at five teams that would be ideal fits for Kucherov as he prepares for the next chapter of his illustrious career.

Right out of the gate, this is the most natural fit of all the potential landing spots. General manager Kent Hughes has done a superb job of locking down his young core on team-friendly contracts, and as a result, the Canadiens have nearly $30 million in projected cap space for next season. They also have a glaring need in their top two lines, and I'd say the reigning Hart Trophy winner would fill that role quite nicely.

Montreal's moment to strike is now. It's an ascendant team with a great salary cap situtation and assets to spend. It's time to make a splash, and this would be a tsunami. Just imagine Kucherov on a power play unit with Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, Lane Hutson and Ivan Demidov. Kucherov would also be coached by former Lightning teammate Martin St. Louis, so a rapport would already exist between player and coach. I expect the Canadiens to do everything in their power to land Kucherov.

We already know the Wild are big-game hunting at forward because they've been heavily linked to former Detroit Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin. If I were advising general manager Bill Guerin -- and I'm certainly not -- I would recommend Minnesota package whatever assets it has offered Detroit and redirect them to Tampa Bay. No, Kucherov is not a center,  and that's the Wild's biggest need.

However, Kucherov is a rare breed of winger in that he can drive play better than most first-line centers from the wing. Put him on a line with Kirill Kaprizov, and the only time opponents will touch the puck is when they're pulling out of the net.

With Quinn Hughes also on an expiring contract, acquiring Kucherov would be a risky move for the Wild. What if they give up premium assets only to lose Kucherov and Hughes next summer? I don't think fear can dictate Minnesota's decisions. The team has a top-two defenseman in the world on its roster right now, and it has the opportunity to acquire a top-five forward. Worry about next summer when the time comes. Go all in to win the Cup while you have a chance.

It was no secret that the Hurricanes were in on the Connor Hellebuyck sweepstakes but just missed out. So, if they can't get better at preventing goals, why not get much better at scoring them? Carolina doesn't exactly need any help offensively, but adding Kucherov would go a long way to helping the team repeat as Stanley Cup champions. Besides, Kucherov would provide another level of playmaking and finishing that the Canes don't currently have on their roster.

Carolina has a good chunk of cap space available already, and it wouldn't need to shed much in order to make room for Kucherov. The Canes also have some enticing young players on their roster that might appeal to the Bolts, and they have three first-round picks over the next two drafts. Why not take a shot at landing a superstar winger?

Similar to the Hurricanes, the Mammoth were in the mix to acquire Hellebucyk, and for good reason. The goaltending tandem of Karel Vejmelka and Sebastian Cossa has not been good, so Utah may have to outscore its problems until one of the goalies finds a groove. Offense may be the best defense for the Mammoth -- and if that's the case -- then Kucherov should be in the mix for the Norris Trophy. There is a great young core of forwards in Salt Lake City, and I think Kucherov would be a perfect fit alongside Logan Cooley, who is emerging as a franchise center.

Utah also has plenty of draft capital with which to work, and it's projected for just over $25 million in salary cap space next season. The Mammoth don't have any major pending free agents on their cap sheet, so they're a suitor capable of signing Kucherov to a long-term extension.

Allow me to get a little bold on the fifth and final destination. The Stars have already failed to sign 27-year-old winger Jason Robertson to a long-term extension once. The two sides agreed to a one-year deal worth $12 million prior to the season, but Robertson's future with the team is still very much in doubt. What if Dallas and Tampa Bay executed a true "hockey trade" -- one player for one player?

Dallas would get the better player in Kucherov, but there are no guarantees regarding an extension. The Stars are in win-now mode, and Kucherov could help them get over the Cup hump immediately. Tampa Bay would get a younger player in Robertson, and although he doesn't have the elite playmaking ability of Kucherov, he's still an exceptionally talented scorer. Perhaps the Bolts could get him to join the team's core and sign a multi-year contract. This deal could work for both sides.
